confirmed.title: `access init` makes the volume root traversable by every grid user but locks down only the admin's own directory
confirmed.scenario: `chmod o+x /rs/rs_grp_oschome` (line 482) lets every grid user traverse the volume root. The only sibling it closes is `$vol/$USER` (line 483). A lab member whose directory was created under umask 022 (for example `/rs/rs_grp_oschome/ab1234` at 2755) was previously shielded because the root was not traversable. `default_root()` also places each member's Ashley ROOT and workspaces there. After init, any grid user can take the member names from `getent group oschome` and run `ls` or `cat /rs/rs_grp_oschome/ab1234/...`. Every other top-level entry on the volume with other-read or other-execute bits is exposed to the whole grid.
confirmed.fix: In init, before `chmod o+x "$vol"`, list `find "$vol" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 ! -path "$SHARED" -perm /o=rwx`. Apply `chmod o-rwx` to the entries the admin owns. Refuse (print the list and exit non-zero) while any entry owned by someone else is still open, so its owner closes it first.

verdict.reason:
The finding holds. In `access init` (grid/ashley:481-484) the code does this:

```
local vol; vol=$(dirname "$(dirname "$LIBRARY_ROOT")")
chmod o+x "$vol" && echo "chmod o+x $vol (traverse only)"
[ -d "$vol/$USER" ] && chmod o-rwx "$vol/$USER" && echo "chmod o-rwx $vol/$USER (your own tree stays private)"
chmod 2771 "$(dirname "$LIBRARY_ROOT")"
```

Before init, only the group could get past the volume root. docs/CHECKPOINT_2026-09-28.md:52 records that init "set `/rs/rs_grp_oschome` 2771 (traverse only)". After init, every grid user can traverse the root.

Only two top-level entries are closed: the admin's own directory (`$vol/$USER`) and `shared/`. Any other entry keeps its own mode bits. The volume root is group-writable (2771), so any member of the oschome group can create `/rs/rs_grp_oschome/<id>`. Under the usual CentOS 7 umask (022 or 002) that directory comes out 2755 or 2775, which is readable and traversable by others.

The code sends members there itself:
- `default_root()` (lines 42-44) picks `/rs/rs_grp_oschome/$USER/ashley` whenever that directory exists and is writable.
- `cmd_adopt` runs `mkdir -p "$ROOT/workspaces"` and binds `/rs/rs_grp_oschome/$USER`.
- `cmd_install` runs `mkdir -p "$ROOT"`.

None of them runs chmod on those directories. So once init has run, any grid user can guess a member id and run `ls` or `cat` on `/rs/rs_grp_oschome/<id>/ashley/workspaces/...`. The ids are predictable, and `getent group oschome` lists them. Before init, the closed root blocked this. The volume root is also not listable by others, so an attacker needs the names, but those are easy to get.

The proposed fix only sweeps the entries that exist when init runs. It is incomplete: a member who creates their directory after init (the normal path through `default_root`) gets o=r-x and is exposed at once. Nothing in the code re-runs init. The fix needs a default ACL on the volume root, and a chmod on the member's own directory, as in the corrected fix below.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In the init step, before `chmod o+x "$vol"`, add:

```
open=$(find "$vol" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 ! -path "$SHARED" -perm /o=rwx)
for e in $open; do [ "$(stat -c %U "$e")" = "$USER" ] && chmod o-rwx "$e"; done
others=$(find "$vol" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 ! -path "$SHARED" -perm /o=rwx)
[ -z "$others" ] || { printf 'still open to all grid users (owner must run chmod o-rwx):\n%s\n' "$others"; exit 1; }
setfacl -d -m u::rwx,g::rwx,o::--- "$vol"   # entries created later under the root start closed to others
```

The default ACL makes mkdir ignore the umask, so new top-level entries get o=---. Directories under them inherit that default ACL. `shared/` already exists, so it is not affected.

Also close the member's own directory whenever Ashley places a ROOT there. In `cmd_install` and `cmd_adopt`, after the ROOT is chosen, add:

```
[ -O "/rs/rs_grp_oschome/$USER" ] && chmod o-rwx "/rs/rs_grp_oschome/$USER"
```

This covers directories created before the default ACL existed.

confirmed.title: The world-writable inbox sits on the lab's quota'd CephFS: any grid user can fill the 20 TB volume, and the ingest keeps the junk
confirmed.scenario: inbox is 1733 and every path component above it is o+x, so any of the grid's users can write there. CephFS quotas are per directory, so the bytes count against the lab's quota, not the writer's. Example: `dd if=/dev/zero of=/rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared/access/inbox/.x bs=1M count=20000000`. The ingest only globs `*.json`, so `.x` is never looked at. Oversized `*.json` files are moved into `requests/` (line 538), not deleted. When the volume fills, every lab job writing to /rs/rs_grp_oschome fails with EDQUOT. Separately, millions of tiny `*.json` files make each ingest (3 to 5 forks per file, run before every admin command) take hours.
confirmed.fix: In `access init`, cap the drop-box with `setfattr -n ceph.quota.max_bytes -v 1048576` and `-n ceph.quota.max_files -v 2000` on the inbox. If the mount's cephx key lacks the p cap, ask C&IT to set these. In the ingest, delete rather than archive anything that is not a valid request, including non-`*.json` names: `find inbox -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 ! -name '*.json' -delete`, and `rm` instead of `mv` on line 538.

verdict.reason:
The finding holds; I could not refute it. In `access init` (grid/ashley), `chmod o+x "$vol"` opens /rs/rs_grp_oschome to traverse, `chmod 2771` does the same for shared/, and line 487 sets `chmod 711 "$ACCESS_ROOT"; chmod 1733 "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox"`. So any grid user can create files, and also subdirectories, in the inbox.

CephFS quotas are per directory tree (ceph.quota.max_bytes on the realm), not per user. Whatever lands in the inbox counts against the lab's 20 TB.

It is worse than the `dd` example. CephFS counts the logical file size, so one `truncate -s <remaining quota> inbox/.x` fills the volume at once without writing any data. After that, every lab job writing under /rs/rs_grp_oschome gets EDQUOT. If the login node's client does not enforce quotas, the file can grow past 20 TB.

The ingest never cleans this up:
- `for f in "$ACCESS_ROOT"/inbox/*.json` skips dotfiles and anything not ending in `.json`.
- A `*.json` file that is too big or wrongly owned is kept: line 538 runs `mv -f "$f" "$ACCESS_ROOT/requests/rejected.${owner:-unknown}.$(date +%s).json"`, which leaves the bytes on the same volume.

The proposed fix is right in direction but incomplete:
1. Deleting in the ingest cannot be what protects the volume. An attacker can `mkdir inbox/.d; chmod 700 inbox/.d` and write inside it. The sticky bit lets the admin, as owner of the inbox, remove entries in the inbox itself, but not the attacker's files inside a 700 directory they own. `rmdir` or `find -delete` then fails on the non-empty directory, and only root can clear it.
2. Deleting a file does not free its space while the attacker keeps a descriptor open.

So the directory quota on the inbox is the only real limit, and it has to exist before the inbox becomes world-writable. `access init` should not quietly carry on without it.

Two more points:
- Setting the quota needs the 'p' MDS capability, which the shared mount's key usually lacks, so C&IT will probably have to set it.
- CephFS quotas are enforced by the client. The kernel client only has quota support from 4.17 on, and a stock CentOS 7 kernel is 3.10. Unless /rs is mounted with ceph-fuse or through NFS-Ganesha, a quota on the inbox may simply not be enforced from the login node. That has to be tested, not assumed.

Even with a working quota, an attacker-owned subdirectory can fill max_files and jam the request mechanism until root removes it. That is much less harmful than a full lab volume, but it is still possible.
verdict.corrected_fix:
1. In `access init`, before `chmod 1733 "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox"`:
   - Try `setfattr -n ceph.quota.max_bytes -v 1048576 "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox"` and `setfattr -n ceph.quota.max_files -v 2000 "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox"`.
   - Check the result with `getfattr -n ceph.quota.max_bytes`. If the attribute is missing or 0 (no 'p' capability), keep the inbox at 0700, print the exact request to send to C&IT, and stop.
   - Also test that the quota is enforced from the login node, for example `truncate -s 2M "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox/.qtest"` must fail with "Disk quota exceeded"; remove `.qtest` afterwards. If it is not enforced (a CentOS 7 3.10 kernel client), do not make the inbox world-writable on this volume at all.
2. In the ingest, delete instead of archive. On line 538, replace the `mv ... || rm` with `rm -f "$f"`.
3. Before the loop, add `find "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 ! -name '*.json' -exec rm -rf {} + 2>/dev/null`. This is housekeeping only: it cannot remove an attacker's non-empty 700 subdirectory or reclaim space held by an open file, which is why the quota in step 1 is required rather than optional.

confirmed.title: The volume root, `shared/` and `shared/ashley` are group-writable, so any oschome member can run code as every student who adopts
confirmed.scenario:
The volume root and `shared/` are 2771 and `shared/ashley` is 2770 or 2775, with no sticky bit. Any oschome member can therefore rename entries they do not own. Two attacks follow:
(a) `mv shared/ashley/library.json x` and put their own `library.json` in its place.
(b) `mv /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared old && mkdir shared`. `access_admin` (line 439) is simply the owner of `shared/`, so the member becomes the 'admin', and students' requests and library lookups go to the member's tree.
Students trust `library.json` completely. `cmd_adopt` writes its `runtime` value into config.env, and the worker job runs `exec "$RUNTIME"` on the host (worker.sbatch.tpl:45). `worker start --container` passes `sandbox` and `claude_bin` unescaped into `sed "s|@SANDBOX@|$w_sandbox|g"` (lines 272-275) and into `W_SANDBOX="@SANDBOX@"`. A value such as `x|g;1e sh -c ...;#` or `$(...)` executes. Result: code runs as each approved student and can read `~/.ashley/secrets.env` and `accounts/*/token` (Claude, GitHub and Hugging Face tokens).
confirmed.fix: Set the sticky bit (`chmod +t`) on `/rs/rs_grp_oschome`, `shared/` and `shared/ashley` in init and in publish, so members can create entries but not rename or replace the admin's. Pin the admin name (`ASHLEY_ADMIN`) instead of deriving it from `stat` of `shared/`. In `cmd_adopt` and `worker start`, refuse a `library.json` that is not owned by that admin or is group- or other-writable. Reject library field values that contain characters outside `[A-Za-z0-9_./-]` before they reach sed or config.

verdict.reason:
The finding holds. I read the code and could not refute it. In grid/ashley, `access init` runs `chmod 2771 "$(dirname "$LIBRARY_ROOT")"` (line 484) and `chmod 2770 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"` (line 485), and `library publish` runs `chmod 2775 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"` (line 76). All three modes give the group rwx and none sets the sticky bit. So any member of the directory's group can rename or replace entries they do not own, such as `shared/ashley/library.json`, `shared/ashley/containers/<name>` or `shared/ashley` itself. Moving an entry within one parent needs only w+x on that parent.

Approved students do not own these entries but trust them fully:
- `cmd_adopt` (lines 82-96) copies `runtime`, `sandbox` and `claude_bin` from `library.json` into config.env.
- `worker start` auto-adopts (line 253).
- worker.sbatch.tpl:45 runs `exec "$RUNTIME" exec ... "$SANDBOX" ... node ...` as the student, with `-B $HOME` bound.

An attacker-chosen runtime runs on the host. A replaced sandbox runs its own `node` inside the container with the student's home mounted. Either way it can read `~/.ashley/secrets.env` and `accounts/*/token`. Students who adopted earlier are also hit: their SANDBOX already points into `$LIBRARY_ROOT/containers/<name>`, which the attacker can swap before their next `worker start`. The sed injection at lines 272-275 through `--container` is also real: GNU sed's `e` command runs the rest of the line. It only matters once `library.json` is attacker-controlled.

Attack (b) depends on the mode of the volume root. The code only adds `o+x` there, so this part is conditional. `access_admin` (line 439) does take the owner of `shared/`, so whoever replaces `shared/` becomes the admin.

The attacker has to be in the unix group. The design expects such people: `admin list` reports `in_group` because C&IT adds lab members on the admin's email.

**Why the proposed fix is incomplete:**

1. The sticky bit protects only direct entries of `shared/ashley`. The `containers/`, `npm-<name>/`, `cache`, `tmp` and similar directories come from the bootstrap job's `mkdir -p`. That job applies only `chmod -R g+rX` and `chmod g+s`, never `g-w`.
2. `acl_grant` runs `setfacl -d -m u:ID:r-X` on `$SHARED` and every directory under it. That creates a default ACL whose base `group::` entry is copied from mode 2770/2771, so it is rwx. From the first approval on, anything the admin creates there, including the `library.json` that python writes as 0666, is group-writable no matter the umask. A member can then edit `library.json` or the sandbox in place, and the sticky bit does not stop that.
3. Checking the owner of `library.json` does not check the sandbox, claude_bin or runtime paths that the file points to.
4. Taking the admin name from `ASHLEY_ADMIN` in the environment is weaker than taking it from the volume-root mount point, which group members cannot rename.
verdict.corrected_fix:
1. **Make the library tree read-only for the group.** In `access init`, and at the end of the publish step in bootstrap.sbatch, after its `chmod -R g+rX`:
   - Run `chmod -R g-w,o-w "$LIBRARY_ROOT"`.
   - Set `shared/ashley` to 2750, not 2770 or 2775, and change line 76 to match.
2. **Stop default ACLs from granting group write.** In `acl_grant`, and once in init, run `setfacl -d -m g::r-X,o::--- "$SHARED"`. Run the same command on each directory under `$LIBRARY_ROOT`.
3. **Add the sticky bit where members must still create entries.** Use `chmod 3771` on `$SHARED`, and `chmod +t` on the volume root, which the admin owns. Members can still add their own folders but cannot rename the admin's.
4. **Pin the admin to something members cannot move.** Change line 439 to `access_admin() { stat -c %U "$(dirname "$SHARED")"; }`, the volume-root mount point.
5. **Check before trusting the library.** In `cmd_adopt` and in `worker start --container`, refuse unless both of these hold:
   - `library.json` is owned by `access_admin` or root, and is not writable by group or other (`stat -c %U`/`%a`, or `find -perm /022`).
   - The same holds for the `sandbox` directory tree, `claude_bin` and `runtime`, and for every parent directory up to `$SHARED`, or up to `/` for system paths such as /usr/bin.
6. **Filter the field values.** Reject any `sandbox`, `claude_bin` or `runtime` value that does not match `^/[A-Za-z0-9_./-]+$` before it reaches `set_cfg` or `sed`.

confirmed.title: `library publish` sets the library back to 2775, opening it to every grid user and bypassing approval
confirmed.scenario: `access init` sets `shared/ashley` to 2770. The next time a lead runs `ashley library publish`, line 76 runs `chmod 2775 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"` (o+rx). `shared/` is o+x, and the sandbox files keep their image modes (644/755), so `library.json` and every container become readable by all grid users. For everyone, `lib_readable` is now true: `worker start` and `install` auto-adopt, and `whoami` reports granted=true without any request. The approval gate no longer does anything.
confirmed.fix: Line 76: use `chmod 2770 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"` (2750 if only the admin publishes), not 2775.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and could not. The scenario works against the code as written.

1. `access init` sets `chmod 2771 "$(dirname "$LIBRARY_ROOT")"` (shared/, o+x) and `chmod 2770 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"` (grid/ashley:484-485). Line 482 also does `chmod o+x "$vol"`. So the only thing keeping other users out of the library is the missing o+rx bits on shared/ashley.

2. `cmd_library publish` runs `mkdir -p "$LIBRARY_ROOT" ...` and then `chmod 2775 "$LIBRARY_ROOT" 2>/dev/null` (grid/ashley:75-76) every time, with no check for an existing mode. The admin owns shared/ashley (they created it, or init ran as the owner), so this chmod succeeds when the admin publishes or re-publishes. Only a non-owner lead's chmod would fail silently. Nothing anywhere puts it back to 2770: the only other chmod calls are in init and install. It does not matter whether init ran before the first publish: if shared/ashley does not exist yet, init's chmod 2770 fails without stopping, and publish then leaves the directory at 2775.

3. Nothing below the directory gates access either. bootstrap.sbatch writes library.json with Python `open(p + ".part", "w")`, so it gets umask modes (normally 644). The sandbox comes from `apptainer build --sandbox` with the image's modes. `containers/` and the npm prefix are made by `mkdir -p` under umask (755). The finishing step, `chmod -R g+rX "$ROOT"; find ... chmod g+s`, only adds group bits and never removes other bits. When a directory has POSIX ACLs, users with no named entry fall under the 'other' class, which is the mode's o bits. With 2775 that is r-x.

4. Result: any grid user can now read library.json, so `lib_readable() { [ -r "$(lib_file)" ]; }` (line 53) is true for them. Then:
   - `cmd_install` auto-adopts (line 124).
   - `worker start` auto-adopts (line 253).
   - `access whoami` and `access status` report `"granted":true` (lines 491, 496-497).
   - `access request` prints "you can already read the shared library" (line 519).
   
   No request is needed, so approval no longer controls anything.

The proposed fix is correct and complete for this defect. Line 76 should match init's 2770. That keeps group write for other leads who publish. chmod on a directory with ACLs sets the ACL mask from the group bits, so rwx keeps approved users' named r-X entries in effect.
verdict.corrected_fix: grid/ashley:76: replace `chmod 2775 "$LIBRARY_ROOT" 2>/dev/null` with `chmod 2770 "$LIBRARY_ROOT" 2>/dev/null` (equivalently `chmod g+rwxs,o-rwx`). Use 2770, not 2750: other leads in the group still need write access to publish, and group bits of rwx keep the ACL mask from masking approved users' r-X entries.

confirmed.title: `acl_grant` follows a symlink placed in `shared/` and grants read on the target tree outside `shared/`, for example the admin's private directory
confirmed.scenario: `for c in "$SHARED"/*` only skips `access`. `setfacl -R` without `-P` follows symlinks given as arguments and recurses into the target. Suppose a member (`shared/` is group-writable) or a careless lead creates `shared/weights -> /rs/rs_grp_oschome/go2432/model_night`, expecting the target's 2750 to keep students out. The next approval of any student runs `setfacl -R -m u:ID:r-X` over the whole go2432 subtree, and the approved non-group student can read the admin's private files. `acl_revoke` follows the same path.
confirmed.fix: In both loops, skip symlinks with `[ -L "$c" ] && continue`, and pass `-P` to `setfacl -R` in `acl_grant` and `acl_revoke`.

verdict.reason:
The bug is real, but the example target in the scenario does not work as written. A link that does work is shown below.

The code (grid/ashley:448-456):
  for c in "$SHARED"/*; do
    [ "$c" = "$ACCESS_ROOT" ] && continue
    [ -e "$c" ] || continue
    setfacl -R -m "u:$1:r-X" "$c" || return 1

Nothing checks whether an entry is a symlink, and `[ -e ]` follows links. By default `setfacl -R` (acl 2.2.51 on CentOS 7) follows symbolic-link arguments and skips only links it finds deeper in the tree. So a top-level link in shared/ sends the recursive grant into its target. `access init` makes shared/ `chmod 2771` (line 484), so any member of the oschome group, or the lead, can create such a link. Non-member users on the node cannot, because they have only x on shared/.

Why the scenario's example fails: `access init` runs `chmod o+x $vol` and `chmod o-rwx $vol/$USER` (lines 482-483). The student can pass through /rs/rs_grp_oschome but not through go2432. With `shared/weights -> /rs/rs_grp_oschome/go2432/model_night`, model_night and everything under it would get u:ID:r-X. But every path to it, the link included, needs search permission on go2432, which the student lacks. So this particular link leaks nothing.

A version that works: `shared/lab -> ../go2432`, or `-> /rs/rs_grp_oschome/go2432`. The grant then lands on go2432 itself, where X means x on directories. The mask is recalculated, so the student gets r-x on go2432 and r on every file under it. Files that are 0600 or 0700 to the group are included, because the mask widens to cover the named user entry. The only parent, /rs/rs_grp_oschome, is o+x, so the student can read the admin's whole private tree. A link to `..` does the same across the whole volume. It hits files owned by other users partway through, so acl_grant returns 1 and the ingest dies. But the admin-owned files already processed keep their ACLs.

acl_revoke (line 463) follows the same link as well.

The proposed fix is correct and enough:
- Add `[ -L "$c" ] && continue` to both loops.
- Use `setfacl -R -P` in acl_grant and acl_revoke. Per the man page, -P "also skips symbolic link arguments", and links deeper in the tree are already skipped by default.
- The `find "$c" -type d` calls need no change, because find does not follow links by default.

What is left is a race: a group member could swap a directory for a link during the walk. That is out of scope, since it needs a hostile group member who can already read go2432 through its group r-x.

confirmed.title: Check-then-use race in the admin's ingest: a student swaps in a FIFO after the `-f` test and hangs every admin command
confirmed.scenario: The student owns `inbox/<id>.json` and can rename their own files inside the sticky inbox at will. They loop, alternating a regular file and a FIFO (created with `mkfifo` in the inbox) under that name. The admin's `-L`/`-f` tests (line 535) see the regular file. `stat` still passes for a FIFO (the owner is the student, the size is 0). Then `grep ... "$f"` on line 541 opens the FIFO and blocks forever. The ingest runs before every `access admin` subcommand (list, approve, deny, reset), and the extension tree calls `accessList` on each refresh. The admin's queue times out and hung bash/grep processes pile up on the login node. Because the status is never written, the student stays at 'none' and can repeat this indefinitely. The same window lets a symlink be followed if `fs.protected_symlinks` is 0: the `note` and `created` strings of any admin-readable file are copied into the student's status.
confirmed.fix: Take the file out of the student's reach first. `mv -f "$f" "$ACCESS_ROOT/requests/.ingest.$$"` is a rename that does not follow links, and `requests/` is 700. Run the `-L`, `-f`, owner and size checks on the moved path, and read it once with `head -c 4096` into a variable before any grep.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute the main scenario. The ingest loop checks the path and later reopens it by name, and the student can change what that name points to in between:
- line 535 `if [ -L "$f" ] || [ ! -f "$f" ]; then rm -f "$f"; continue; fi`
- line 536 `owner=$(stat -c %U "$f")`
- line 537 `stat -c %s "$f"` must be at most 4096
- line 540 `status_state "$u"` must be none
- line 541 `n=$(grep -o '"note": ...' "$f" | ...)`

The inbox is mode 1733, sticky and world-writable. The student owns `inbox/<id>.json`, so they can `mkfifo inbox/.t; mv -f inbox/.t inbox/<id>.json` and replace their own file at any moment. The sticky bit allows this because they own the target.

Once the FIFO is in place, every later check still passes:
- `stat` never opens the file, so the owner comes back as the student.
- The size is 0.
- `status_state` answers none, because no status file exists yet.

GNU grep reads a FIFO named on its command line without O_NONBLOCK, so the grep on line 541 blocks in open() for good; the student simply never opens a writer. The `c=$(grep ...)` on the same line gives a second window.

The window runs from line 535 to line 541 and spans four or five fork/execs. The student does not have to swap blindly. The process list is visible to other users, so they can watch for the admin's `stat -c %U .../inbox/<id>.json` and swap the moment it appears, which makes winning the race close to deterministic.

The loop runs before every `access admin` subcommand. `tree.ts:113` calls `accessList()` on each refresh for the admin. That call gives up after 60 s on the laptop, but on the grid the bash/grep pair stays blocked in open(). No pty is attached, so nothing sends SIGHUP, and the blocked processes pile up. `write_status` is never reached, so the student stays at none and can keep doing this.

Two overstatements. First, "hangs every admin command" is too strong: a run where the check itself sees the FIFO goes through line 535, which deletes it (the admin owns the inbox). Only runs where the swap lands inside the window hang, but with the process-list trick the student can make that most of them. Second, the symlink variant only works if `fs.protected_symlinks` is 0. CentOS 7 defaults it to 1, which stops the admin from following a symlink the student owns in the admin's sticky directory. So that part is conditional, as the finding says.

The proposed fix is sound. A rename does not follow links and does not open the file. Once the file is in `requests/` (mode 700), the student can no longer reach it by name. Reading it once with `head -c 4096` bounds what a writer holding an open descriptor can do. Two small gaps are worth closing, and they are in `corrected_fix`:
- Use `mv -T`, so that a leftover `.ingest.<pid>` directory from a reused PID is not treated as a destination.
- Use `rm -rf` for anything that is not a regular file. A directory the student created as `<id>.json` would otherwise stay behind in `requests/`.
verdict.corrected_fix:
At the top of the loop body (after line 533), take the file out of the inbox before any test, then run every test on the private copy:

```
local t="$ACCESS_ROOT/requests/.ingest.$$"
rm -rf -- "$t"
mv -fT -- "$f" "$t" 2>/dev/null || continue   # rename: does not follow links or open the file; requests/ is 700
if [ -L "$t" ] || [ ! -f "$t" ]; then rm -rf -- "$t"; continue; fi
owner=$(stat -c %U -- "$t" 2>/dev/null)
if [ "$owner" != "$u" ] || ! getent passwd "$u" >/dev/null || [ "$(stat -c %s -- "$t")" -gt 4096 ]; then
  mv -fT -- "$t" "$ACCESS_ROOT/requests/rejected.${owner:-unknown}.$(date +%s).json" 2>/dev/null || rm -f -- "$t"; continue
fi
[ "$(status_state "$u")" = none ] || { rm -f -- "$t"; continue; }
local body; body=$(head -c 4096 -- "$t")
n=$(printf '%s' "$body" | grep -o '"note": *"[^"]*"' | head -1 | sed 's/.*"\([^"]*\)"$/\1/')
c=$(printf '%s' "$body" | grep -o '"created": *"[^"]*"' | head -1 | sed 's/.*"\([^"]*\)"$/\1/')
mv -fT -- "$t" "$ACCESS_ROOT/requests/$u.$(date +%s).json" 2>/dev/null
write_status "$u" pending "$n" "" "$c"
```

`u` is still taken from the basename of the original `$f`.

confirmed.title: Status files, and request files while they sit in the inbox, are readable by anyone who knows or guesses the AccessID

AccessIDs are two letters and four digits and can be collected from `squeue -a`, `ps` or `/home`, or brute-forced with stat. The names are grid AccessIDs such as go2432, and any login-node user can collect them from getent passwd, /home, squeue or ps. The file's group is inherited through the setgid bit on shared/, and 644 is also group-readable, so every oschome member can read these files too. The CHECKPOINT (docs/CHECKPOINT_2026-09-28.md line 54) records that `access init` at 03:53 set `status 755`, which is listable. (2) On deny/remove, `setfacl` on an id that is not in passwd would fail. Nothing checks getent for deny/remove, so chaining it with `&&` would silently skip writing the status. Writing to a `.part` name first and renaming it avoids this: the glob only matches `*.json`, and the student may rename their own file in the sticky directory.

  printf ... > "$(status_file "$1").part" || return 1
  setfacl -m "u:$1:r" "$(status_file "$1").part" 2>/dev/null   # tolerate ids not in passwd (deny/remove do not check getent)

confirmed.title: Control characters in a hand-written request pass through `json_str` unescaped: the admin's queue appears empty and the CLI prints terminal escape sequences
confirmed.scenario: A student writes `inbox/<id>.json` by hand with `"note": "hi\x1b]0;x\x07"` (raw bytes). `grep -o '"note": *"[^"]*"'` keeps the ESC and BEL bytes, and `json_str` (lines 27-29) escapes only backslash, quote, newline, CR and tab, so the bytes go raw into the status file. `access admin list --json` then emits invalid JSON: `JSON.parse` throws 'Bad control character', `parseLastJson` returns null, and `accessList` returns []. The admin's panel and tree show '0 pending, 0 approved' for everyone, and the offending row cannot be seen in order to reset it. In a terminal, `ashley access admin list` `cat`s the raw escape sequences, which can set the title, rewrite lines, or write the clipboard via OSC 52 on some terminals. The `created` field has the same problem.
confirmed.fix: In the ingest, sanitise both fields: `n=$(... | tr -d '\000-\037\177' | cut -c1-500)`, and the same for `c`. Also make `json_str` strip the remaining C0 control characters and DEL.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and could not. The scenario works as written.

1. **The request passes ingest.** Any grid user can traverse to `inbox/`, which is mode 1733. There they can create `inbox/<own id>.json`: a regular file under 4096 bytes, owned by the user it names, with raw ESC (0x1b) and BEL (0x07) bytes inside the note. It passes every ingest check (lines 533-539: not a symlink, owner equals the name, user exists, size limit, state is none). No hand-editing is needed either: `ashley access request --note "$(printf 'x\033]0;y\007')"` writes the same bytes. `json_str` (lines 27-29) does not escape them:
   `local s=${1//\\/\\\\}; s=${s//\"/\\\"}; s=${s//$'\n'/\\n}; s=${s//$'\r'/}; s=${s//$'\t'/\\t}; printf '"%s"' "$s"`

2. **The bytes survive extraction.** Line 541 pulls the note out with `n=$(grep -o '"note": *"[^"]*"' "$f" | head -1 | sed 's/.*"\([^"]*\)"$/\1/')`. The same pattern is used for `c` ("created"). GNU grep treats a file as binary only on NUL bytes (and, from 2.21, on encoding errors), so ESC and BEL are printed, and `[^"]*` matches them. Line 543 then runs `write_status "$u" pending "$n" "" "$c"`, which puts both values through `json_str`. The raw bytes land in `status/<u>.json`.

3. **The admin's JSON listing breaks.** `admin list --json` (line 556) runs `tr -d '\n' < "$f" | sed 's/}$//'` over every status file and joins them into one line. `JSON.parse` rejects raw U+0000–U+001F inside a string literal ("Bad control character in string literal"). `parseLastJson` (gridApi.ts:224) catches the error and returns null. `accessList` (gridApi.ts:75) returns `|| []`. So `commandAccess` (extension.ts:466) and the tree (tree.ts:113) both show "0 pending, 0 approved". Every row disappears, not only the attacker's, and the admin cannot pick the bad row in order to reset it.

4. **The terminal listing prints raw escapes.** The plain listing (line 558) runs `cat "$f"` on each status file, which sends ESC/OSC sequences straight to the admin's terminal: title changes, cursor movement and line rewriting, and clipboard writes via OSC 52 on terminals that allow it.

A student cannot write status files (they are written by the admin, and `status/` is 711), so everything in them comes through `write_status`, and therefore through `json_str`. That makes `json_str` the essential fix. The ingest `tr` in the proposed fix is harmless, but it does not cover a status file that is already poisoned, and on its own it would leave the problem in place for every other caller of `json_str`. The proposed `tr -d '\000-\037\177'` is fine for the single-line ingest fields. Inside `json_str`, though, it must keep \t and \n or delete them only after they have been escaped, so the fix below uses a narrower range.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Strip control characters inside `json_str`, before escaping, keeping \t and \n (which are escaped afterwards). This one change covers ingest, `request --note`, and every other writer:

json_str() { # escape a string for JSON; drop C0 controls (except \t \n) and DEL
  local s; s=$(printf '%s' "$1" | LC_ALL=C tr -d '\000-\010\013\014\016-\037\177')
  s=${s//\\/\\\\}; s=${s//\"/\\\"}; s=${s//$'\n'/\\n}; s=${s//$'\r'/}; s=${s//$'\t'/\\t}; printf '"%s"' "$s"
}

You can also cap the length at ingest (line 541) as extra protection: append `| LC_ALL=C tr -d '\000-\037\177' | cut -c1-500` to the `n=` and `c=` pipelines.

A status file already poisoned before this fix is not repaired by it. On the next `admin` run, rewrite each status file once through `write_status`. Alternatively, make the `--json` list filter every file with `LC_ALL=C tr -d '\000-\037\177'` instead of `tr -d '\n'`, and pipe the plain `cat "$f"` through the same `tr`, which also protects the terminal.

confirmed.title: Remove/deny reports success while ACLs survive on anything the admin does not own; approve stops midway and leaves partial grants
confirmed.scenario: Only a file's owner can change its ACL. Leads are expected to publish, and new entries inherit the default ACL `u:ID:r-X` from `shared/`. For example, a lead creates `shared/leadproject` or publishes a container, and it inherits `u:X:r-X`. On `admin remove X`, `setfacl -R -x` hits EPERM on the lead's files. `acl_revoke` sends errors to `2>/dev/null` and returns 0, so the status says 'removed'. Because `shared/` is o+x, X keeps reading `shared/leadproject`. In the other direction, `acl_grant` hits the same EPERM and returns 1 after already granting `shared/` and earlier children. The script dies before `write_status`, so the student has partial access while the queue still says pending.
confirmed.fix: After revoking, verify: `getfacl -R -P -p "$SHARED" 2>/dev/null | grep -q "^user:$1:"`. If anything is left, print where and exit non-zero instead of claiming success. At the start of `acl_grant`, refuse if `find "$SHARED" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 ! -user "$USER"` lists anything. If a grant fails, call `acl_revoke` so no partial grant is left behind.

verdict.reason:
I tried to refute this and could not. The scenario works against the code as written. The approve half is real too, but it is a consistency and availability problem rather than a leak.

1. **Other people can create entries under shared/.** `access init` sets shared/ to `chmod 2771` (group rwx, others x) and LIBRARY_ROOT to 2770. `library publish` ("leads only") runs as whoever calls it: `mkdir -p "$LIBRARY_ROOT"`, then a bootstrap job writes the sandbox. That job also rewrites library.json with `os.replace`, so the file ends up owned by that user (bootstrap.sbatch records `built_by: $USER`). So any oschome group member other than the admin can own entries under shared/.

2. **New entries inherit the student's grant.** acl_grant (line 449) sets `setfacl -d -m "u:$1:r-X" "$SHARED"`. A lead's later `mkdir shared/leadproject` therefore inherits `u:X:r-x`, owned by the lead. Because the default ACL is filled out from 2771, it also gets `other::--x`.

3. **Revoke fails silently and still reports success.** Only the owner (or CAP_FOWNER) may change an ACL. acl_revoke (lines 458-465) runs `setfacl -R -x "u:$1" "$c" 2>/dev/null ... return 0`, so the EPERM is discarded. Then deny/remove (line 566) does `acl_revoke "$id"; write_status ... removed`. X loses the named entry on shared/ but falls back to "other", which has x on shared/ (2771). X can still reach `shared/leadproject` by the name it already knows and read it through the entry that survived. `reset` (line 568) has the same flaw.

4. **Approve stops midway.** acl_grant runs `setfacl -m ... "$SHARED" && setfacl -d -m ... || return 1` first, then `setfacl -R -m "u:$1:r-X" "$c" || return 1` in the loop. GNU setfacl keeps going after EPERM and exits 1 at the end. So the grants on shared/, on earlier children, and on the admin-owned files inside the failing child all remain. Line 561 then dies (`die "setfacl failed"`) before write_status, so the status still says pending.

   This fires on the documented path: a lead publishes into an admin-owned shared/ashley, and the lead-owned sandbox files sit at depth 2 or more. From then on every approve dies.

**Why the proposed fix is incomplete or wrong:**
- The depth-1 `find ! -user` refusal misses exactly that path, because the lead-owned files are deeper. setfacl -R still fails, so with rollback added the admin can never approve anyone again.
- `getfacl -R` over the whole tree flags lead-owned deep files even where X is already cut off by an admin-owned 2770 parent. Remove would then always "fail" and never write status, although nothing leaks. The admin cannot clear this without the lead.

The real flaw is that the security boundary is spread across files that only their owners can change. It exists because shared/ must stay o+x for shared/access to be reachable.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Make the boundary one directory the admin owns and that has no access for "other". Then revoke needs only a single setfacl that is guaranteed to work:

1. Move the drop-box out of shared/: `ACCESS_ROOT="$(dirname "$SHARED")/access"`, which is /rs/rs_grp_oschome/access with the same 711 / 1733 / 711 / 700 modes. The volume root is already o+x. In `access init`, use `chmod 2770 "$SHARED"` instead of 2771. ACCESS_ROOT is referenced only inside grid/ashley.

2. acl_revoke: the gate step must succeed and must be verified.
   `setfacl -x "u:$1" "$SHARED" && setfacl -d -x "u:$1" "$SHARED" || return 1; getfacl -cp "$SHARED" | grep -q "^user:$1:" && return 1`
   Then clean up the tree best-effort, ignoring errors. X now falls to "other" on shared/, which has no x, so nothing underneath is reachable whoever owns it. deny/remove/reset must use `acl_revoke "$id" || die "could not revoke $id on $SHARED"` before write_status.

3. acl_grant: grant on $SHARED plus its default ACL. If that fails, call acl_revoke and return 1. Make the recursive child grant best-effort: collect the paths setfacl could not change (files owned by others) and print them as a warning rather than dying. Then write_status approved, so a lead's files never block approvals or leave partial grants with a stale "pending".

If shared/access must stay where it is, the minimum instead is:
- Verify, not suppress, removal of `u:$1` on $SHARED and on each depth-1 child.
- Require each depth-1 child other than access to be owned by the admin and to have no other-x. Note that `library publish`'s `chmod 2775 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"` breaks this and must become 2770.
- Treat EPERM deeper down as a warning, not a failure.

confirmed.title: The predictable inbox filename lets any user block a given student (or all students) from filing
confirmed.scenario: Attacker A creates `inbox/ab1234.json` (or a symlink) before B does. In the sticky directory B cannot overwrite or remove A's file, so B's `printf > inbox/ab1234.json` fails with 'cannot write the request'. The admin's next ingest rejects A's file, but A recreates it in a loop and can do so for every AccessID from `squeue` or `/home`. Nobody can file a request.
confirmed.fix: Create each request under an unpredictable name with O_EXCL: `f=$(mktemp -p "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox" --suffix=.json "$USER.XXXXXXXX")`. In the ingest, take `u=${name%%.*}` for the owner check. Status stays keyed on `u`.

verdict.reason:
The scenario works against the code as written. `access init` sets `chmod 1733 "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox"`, so any user can create a file in the inbox, and the sticky bit stops anyone other than the file's owner or the directory owner from removing or renaming it. The student writes to a fixed, guessable name: `printf '{"user":...}' ... > "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox/$USER.json" || die "cannot write the request"` (line 525). There is no O_EXCL, no random name, and no retry.

If attacker A runs `touch inbox/ab1234.json` first (mode 644, owned by A), B's `>` redirection hits EACCES and B gets "cannot write the request". If A instead makes the file 666, B's write succeeds and B is told "request filed". The ingest then rejects the file because of `[ "$owner" != "$u" ]` (the owner is A) and moves it to `rejected.A.*`, so B's status stays `none` with no warning to B. A symlink planted by A fails for B under CentOS 7's `protected_symlinks=1`, which is still a block.

The admin ingest does clear the planted file, but only when the admin next opens the queue. The directory stays world-writable, so a loop run by A (`while :; do touch inbox/ab1234.json; sleep 1; done`) re-plants it right away. A can target every id listed by squeue or /home. The extension's admin QuickPick only acts on rows that have a status file, so a blocked student never shows up there. The only way around it is a manual `ashley access admin approve ID` from the CLI. The finding holds, and "low" is the right severity.

The proposed fix is on the right track but incomplete:
1. mktemp always creates the file with mode 0600, whatever the umask. The admin is not root and could not read the note or created fields: the ingest's `grep ... "$f"` would return nothing and the archived request in `requests/` would be unreadable. A `chmod 644` is required. The name is unpredictable and the directory cannot be listed, so 644 exposes nothing.
2. `u=${name%%.*}` cuts a username that contains a dot at the first dot, so a legitimate request from such a user would be rejected. Stripping only the random component is safer.
3. Writing into the final `*.json` name after mktemp opens a window in which the ingest can take an empty file. Creating the file as `.part` and renaming it keeps the current atomic-publish pattern. The ingest globs only `*.json`, and the rename target has an unpredictable name.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In `request` (grid/ashley:525), replace the direct redirection with:
  local f; f=$(mktemp -p "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox" --suffix=.part "$USER.XXXXXXXXXX") || die "cannot write the request"
  chmod 644 "$f"   # mktemp makes 0600; the admin (not root) must be able to read it
  printf '{"user":%s,...}\n' ... > "$f" && mv "$f" "${f%.part}.json" || { rm -f "$f"; die "cannot write the request"; }
In the admin ingest (line ~534), take the owner id by stripping only the random part:
  u=$(basename "$f" .json); u=${u%.*}
Keep the existing owner, symlink and size checks. Status stays keyed on `u`. Optionally, have the ingest also delete stale `*.part` files older than a day.

confirmed.title: `library publish` sets the library back to 2775 (world-readable), which undoes `access init` and grants everyone
confirmed.scenario: `access init` sets shared/ashley to 2770. The admin's next `ashley library publish` (for example, a Claude Code update) runs `chmod 2775 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"` again. That gives others r-x on shared/ashley, and shared (2771) and the volume (o+x) are already traversable. If nobody has been approved yet, library.json is written with the job's 0644 umask. From then on `lib_readable` is true for every account on the grid. `access whoami` reports granted=true, stepLabAccess.check reports 'granted', and `install` and `worker start` adopt the shared container with no request at all. After approvals exist, library.json inherits other::--- from the default ACL, but the sandboxes built earlier keep the image's o+r modes, so anyone who knows the path can still run them.
confirmed.fix: Line 76: change `chmod 2775` to `chmod 2770`. Better, only chmod when publish has just created the directory, so a republish never loosens what `access init` set.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute it. grid/ashley:76, inside `library publish`, runs `chmod 2775 "$LIBRARY_ROOT" 2>/dev/null` every time, with no check on whether the directory already existed. The only other place that sets this mode is `access init` (line 485, `chmod 2770 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"`), which runs once. The documented order in docs/INSTALL.md is publish, then `access init`, so the first publish is harmless. Any later publish by the admin (the volume owner, so the chmod succeeds) sets shared/ashley back to o+r-x. The path above it stays traversable: init ran `chmod o+x "$vol"` and `chmod 2771` on shared/.

The bootstrap job then rewrites library.json as a new file (`json.dump(... open(p + ".part","w"))` followed by `os.replace`). If shared/ashley has no default ACL (nobody approved yet), the file's mode comes from the umask Slurm passes to the job, 022 or 002, so it is o+r. `lib_readable() { [ -r "$(lib_file)" ]; }` then returns true for every account on the grid, and each of these follows:

The approval step is skipped entirely.

After an approval, acl_grant has put a default ACL on shared/ashley while it was 2770, so a rewritten library.json gets other::---. But the directory itself is still o+r-x, so anyone can list it. containers/ and npm-NAME/ were made by earlier jobs with umask modes (and `chmod -R g+rX` never removes other bits), and the sandbox keeps the image's o+rx modes. Any user can therefore find the sandbox and run it by path.

The proposed fix (2770 at line 76, or chmod only when publish creates the directory) is right and closes both routes, because others can no longer traverse into shared/ashley, whatever the file modes inside. One gap: changing the code does not repair a directory that a past publish already opened. The admin should re-run `ashley access init`, which re-applies 2770 and is safe to repeat.
verdict.corrected_fix: grid/ashley line 76: change `chmod 2775 "$LIBRARY_ROOT" 2>/dev/null` to `chmod 2770 "$LIBRARY_ROOT" 2>/dev/null`. This fits the "group-readable" comment at line 71, and approved users still read through their ACL entries, since the chmod sets the ACL mask to rwx. The narrower version also works: `[ -d "$LIBRARY_ROOT" ] || { mkdir -p "$LIBRARY_ROOT" && chmod 2770 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"; }`, followed by `mkdir -p "$ASHLEY_HOME/log"`. confirmed.title: A failed adopt exits the whole script silently, and the wizard reports 'granted; you use the lab's shared container' anyway
confirmed.scenario: `cmd_adopt` reports errors with `die`, which calls `exit 1` in the main shell. The `&& ... ; then` at line 124 and the call at line 253 therefore never fall through, and both send stderr to /dev/null. This happens when library.json is readable but the default sandbox or claude_bin is not: for example during acl_grant's walk, or after an approve that aborted partway (see the setfacl finding). In that state `ashley install` prints only 'installed ashley ...' and exits 1. gridInstall.run then fails with no reason given. `worker start` exits 1 with no output, so the extension shows an empty error. stepLabAccess.check (wizard.ts:511-514) runs `ashley install`, ignores its exit code and returns 'done' with 'granted; you use the lab's shared container'. The wizard then shows 'Setup finished', but the student has no container.
confirmed.fix: Call adopt in a subshell so `die` cannot kill the caller, and let stderr through. Line 124: `lib_readable && ( cmd_adopt "$(lib_default)" ); then`. Line 253: `( cmd_adopt "$(lib_default)" ) >/dev/null; load_cfg`. The state lives in files, so nothing is lost. In stepLabAccess.check, look at the install exit code (or re-read `status --json`.ready) and return 'todo' with the install's stderr when it is not ready.

verdict.reason:
The finding is real. I could not refute it.

**`die` kills the caller.** `die() { echo "ashley: $*" >&2; exit 1; }` (grid/ashley:26). The script sets `set -uo pipefail` but not `-e`. A bash function that runs `exit` inside an `if` condition ends the whole script, not just the function. There are two call sites:
- Line 124: `if [ $build_own -eq 0 ] && lib_readable && cmd_adopt "$(lib_default)" 2>/dev/null; then return 0; fi`. The author clearly expected a failed adopt to return false and fall through to the AWAITING_ACCESS or bootstrap branch. Instead, install prints only `installed ashley ...`, exits 1, and the reason goes to /dev/null.
- Line 253: `if ! is_ready && lib_readable; then cmd_adopt "$(lib_default)" >/dev/null 2>&1; load_cfg; fi`. `worker start` exits 1 with no output. gridApi.workerStart then returns `message: (r.stdout + r.stderr).trim()`, which is the empty string.

**When the library is readable but adopt dies.** `lib_readable` only tests `-r library.json`. `cmd_adopt` then dies on `[ -x "$sandbox/usr/local/bin/node" ]` or `[ -r "$claude" ]` (lines 89-90). Two ways to get there:
1. During `acl_grant`, while `setfacl -R -m u:ID:r-X shared/ashley` is still walking. The walk visits directory entries in readdir order, so library.json can be granted before the sandbox and npm trees, which hold thousands of files.
2. After an approve that stopped partway. `acl_grant` returns 1 on the first setfacl failure. For example, the default container was published by another group member, so the admin cannot setfacl their files, while library.json is admin-owned (os.replace by the admin's later publish). The approve dies, `write_status` never runs, and library.json keeps its ACL. The state persists.

**The extension reports success anyway.** stepLabAccess.check (wizard.ts:511-514):
```
if (j.granted) {
  await ssh(..., ['~/.ashley/bin/ashley', 'install'], ...);
  return report(this.id, this.title, 'done', "granted; you use the lab's shared container");
```
It ignores the result. `granted` is just `lib_readable` (line 491). Through `commandAccess`, the student path of "Ashley: Lab access" runs `runWizard({only:['labAccess']})` and calls `p.finish('...granted; you use the lab\'s shared container', true)`, which is a success screen while the student has no container.

**One detail in the finding is overstated.** The full setup wizard does not normally reach "Setup finished". stepGridInstall.check comes first and sees ready=false with library=true, so `awaiting=false` and no bootstrap job. confirmed.title: acl_grant stops at the first file the admin does not own: approve fails for everyone and leaves partial ACLs with the request still pending
confirmed.scenario: shared/ is 2771 and shared/ashley is 2770, so every oschome group member can write there, and the publish help says 'leads only' (plural). Once a second lead runs `ashley library publish` (containers/<name> is then owned by that lead), or any member drops a file into shared/, every approve fails the same way. setfacl gets EPERM on the foreign files, `setfacl -R` exits 1 and `|| return 1` fires. By then $SHARED and part of that child already carry u:ID entries. The `find ... setfacl -d` for that child and all later children are skipped, so containers published later do not inherit. `die` then leaves the status at 'pending'. The student may already see granted=true (library.json got its entry) while their status says pending and the sandbox is unreadable. Retrying fails again.
confirmed.fix: Do not abort on files the admin cannot change. Walk only the admin's own files, for example `find "$c" -user "$USER" -exec setfacl -m "u:$1:r-X" {} +` plus the same for `-type d` with `-d -m`, and print a count of the foreign files skipped. Alternatively, make shared and shared/ashley 2751/2750 in `access init` so only the admin can create entries there.

verdict.reason:
The finding holds against grid/ashley as written. `access init` sets the modes at lines 484-485 (`chmod 2771` on shared/, `chmod 2770` on shared/ashley), so every oschome group member has group rwx on both. The admin page drafts the email asking C&IT to add approved students to oschome, so every approved student ends up with that write access too. The only thing restricting `library publish` is a comment (line 71, "leads only"); nothing checks is_admin.

Another member's publish leaves files that user owns under shared/ashley. bootstrap.sbatch creates `$ROOT/npm-$LIB_NAME` and cache/tmp entries as that user. Its python step does `os.replace` on library.json, so the file becomes theirs. It does this even when the build later fails.

acl_grant (lines 448-456) runs `setfacl -R -m "u:$1:r-X" "$c" || return 1`. Only the owner can change a file's ACL, so every file owned by someone else returns EPERM. GNU setfacl -R keeps walking the tree, then exits 1. By then $SHARED and every admin-owned file in that child already carry the u:ID entry. `return 1` then skips the `find ... setfacl -d` for that child and for every later child, so directories created later do not inherit.

Line 561 is `acl_grant "$id" || die "setfacl failed for $id"`, so write_status never runs and the state stays pending. If library.json is still admin-owned, lib_readable is true and whoami/status report granted=true while the state says pending. Each retry hits the same files, so every approve fails until those files are removed or chowned.

The first proposed fix is right in direction but incomplete:
- setfacl follows symlink arguments by default. `find -user $USER -exec setfacl` would pass admin-owned symlinks inside a container sandbox to setfacl, which would then change the target on the host. Those symlinks must be excluded.
- The fix should also skip a symlink at the top of shared/. The current code already has a related hole here: a group member can run `ln -s /rs/rs_grp_oschome/go2432 shared/zz`, and the next approve's `setfacl -R` follows that symlink argument and grants r-X on the admin's whole private tree.

The alternative (2751/2750 in init) is insufficient on its own. It leaves foreign files already present in place. The admin's own `ashley library publish` also runs `chmod 2775 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"` (line 76), which gives group write back.

Foreign-owned files cannot be opened by the admin without root. They should be reported, not treated as a failure. Default ACLs set on the admin's directories cover files anyone creates in them later.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In grid/ashley, replace acl_grant with a version that changes only the admin's own non-symlink entries, never aborts on entries owned by someone else, and reports how many it skipped:

acl_grant() { # ID
  setfacl -m "u:$1:r-x" "$SHARED" && setfacl -d -m "u:$1:r-X" "$SHARED" || return 1
  local c skipped=0
  for c in "$SHARED"/*; do
    [ "$c" = "$ACCESS_ROOT" ] && continue
    [ -L "$c" ] && continue            # setfacl follows symlink arguments; never follow one out of shared/
    [ -e "$c" ] || continue
    find "$c" -user "$USER" ! -type l -exec setfacl -m "u:$1:r-X" {} + 2>/dev/null
    find "$c" -user "$USER" -type d -exec setfacl -d -m "u:$1:r-X" {} + 2>/dev/null
    skipped=$(( skipped + $(find "$c" ! -user "$USER" ! -type l 2>/dev/null | wc -l) ))
  done
  [ "$skipped" -eq 0 ] || echo "note: $skipped entries in $SHARED are owned by other users and were left unchanged; their owners must run setfacl -m u:$1:r-X on them (or chown them to $USER)" >&2
  return 0
}

Also add `[ -L "$c" ] && continue` to acl_revoke's loop. Separately, line 76 (`chmod 2775 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"`) should be 2770 or removed, so that publishing does not undo the layout `access init` set.

confirmed.title: Another user can squat inbox/<victim>.json and block or silently void the victim's single request
confirmed.scenario: The inbox is 1733 and the request goes to a predictable path. Any account can run `touch /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared/access/inbox/ab1234.json`. The victim's `access request` then gets EACCES ('cannot write the request') and cannot delete the file, because the directory is sticky. If the squatter makes the file 0666 instead, the victim's write succeeds and prints 'request filed'. The file is still owned by the attacker, so ingest (line 536) moves it to rejected, and the victim's state stays 'none' without them being told. A loop over `getent passwd` names re-squats every account after each ingest.
confirmed.fix: Create the request under a unique name with O_EXCL (`f=$(mktemp "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox/req.XXXXXXXX") && chmod 644 "$f"`) and write into it. At ingest, take the user from `stat -c %U "$f"` instead of from the file name. The one-request rule still holds, because ingest checks status_state of the owner.

verdict.reason:
The finding holds against the code as written. `access init` makes the drop-box reachable and writable by every account on the system: `chmod o+x "$vol"`, shared at 2771, access at 711 and `chmod 1733 "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox"`. The request is always written to a name anyone can predict (line 525):
`... > "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox/$USER.json" || die "cannot write the request"`

**Variant A (the victim is blocked).** An attacker runs `touch inbox/ab1234.json` first, leaving the file at 0644 and owned by the attacker. The victim's `>` redirect then opens that existing file with O_TRUNC, has no write bit on it, gets EACCES, and dies with "cannot write the request". The sticky bit on inbox means the victim cannot delete the attacker's file.

**Variant B (the request is silently voided).** The attacker makes the file 0666 instead. The victim's write then succeeds and prints "request filed". Ingest checks the owner:
`owner=$(stat -c %U "$f") ; if [ "$owner" != "$u" ] ... mv -f "$f" "$ACCESS_ROOT/requests/rejected.${owner:-unknown}...json"`
So the file is moved to rejected and `write_status` is never called. On its next check, the wizard's `stepLabAccess.check` reports only "not requested yet", with no reason given.

**The attack repeats.** Ingest runs at the top of every `access admin` call, including list. It removes the squatted file, and an attacker loop over `getent passwd` names simply re-creates it. The loop also needs no timing: the victim may file at any moment, so the attacker only has to keep the file in place. A CentOS 7 kernel (3.10) has no `fs.protected_regular`, so nothing blocks either variant. On a newer kernel with that setting, variant B would turn into variant A, which is still a denial of service.

**The extension is unaffected by a rename.** It goes through `ashley access request` (wizard.ts:548) and never relies on the `$USER.json` name, so changing the file name breaks nothing on that side.

**The proposed fix is right in principle but incomplete as written:**
1. `mktemp "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox/req.XXXXXXXX"` makes a file with no `.json` suffix, and ingest only globs `inbox/*.json`. Requests made this way would never be ingested.
2. `mktemp` creates an empty file that is then written in place. An ingest that runs between the two steps would accept an empty request, with no note and no creation time. The student's redirect would then re-create the path, and the next ingest would delete that copy because the status is already pending.

Writing to a random `.part` name and renaming it to `.json` fixes both problems. The name is random and the directory is not listable, so no one can squat either name. The student owns the file, so the sticky bit still lets them rename it.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Request side (replace line 525):
```
local f; f=$(mktemp "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox/req.XXXXXXXXXX.part") || die "cannot write the request"
chmod 644 "$f"   # mktemp makes 0600; the admin is not root and must read it
printf '{"user":%s,...}\n' ... > "$f" && mv -f "$f" "${f%.part}.json" || { rm -f "$f"; die "cannot write the request"; }
```
(GNU mktemp in coreutils 8.22 on CentOS 7 treats the `.part` after the X's as `--suffix`.)

Ingest side (lines 533-537): take the user from the file's owner, not from its name.
```
[ -e "$f" ] || [ -L "$f" ] || continue
if [ -L "$f" ] || [ ! -f "$f" ]; then rm -f "$f"; continue; fi
local u; u=$(stat -c %U "$f" 2>/dev/null)
if [ -z "$u" ] || ! getent passwd "$u" >/dev/null || [ "$(stat -c %s "$f")" -gt 4096 ]; then
  mv -f "$f" "$ACCESS_ROOT/requests/rejected.${u:-unknown}.$(date +%s).json" 2>/dev/null || rm -f "$f"; continue
fi
```
The rest of the loop stays as it is. The existing `[ "$(status_state "$u")" = none ] || rm -f "$f"` check still enforces one request per owner, including duplicates filed before one ingest runs. An account whose uid has no name comes back from stat as `UNKNOWN`, fails `getent`, and is rejected. Files the owner renames from `.part` to `.json` are the only ones ingest ever sees.

- `whoami --json` reports `"state":"none"`.
- `check` falls through to `return report(..., 'todo', 'not requested yet')` (wizard.ts:522).
- tree.ts:117 shows 'request it once everything else is set up'.
- `runWizard` calls `run()` on any non-done check. `run()` asks again 'One request to your lead (you can ask once)', then `access request` passes `[ "$st" = none ]` and overwrites the student's own file in the sticky inbox.

If the admin approves before `library.json` exists, or it is later written with a mode that masks the inherited ACL, whoami returns state `approved` with `granted` false. `check` has no `approved` branch and says 'not requested yet'. `run()` then asks for a note, and the grid dies with "you already have a request on file (state: approved); ask your lead to reset it". (c) Denied or removed. `check` returns `'failed'`. `runWizard` skips only on `pre.status === 'done'`, so it calls `run()`. Severity: low, UX only. No security impact.

The proposed fix is right in substance, with one trap. `status_state` is also called by the admin ingest loop: `[ "$(status_state "$u")" = none ] || { rm -f "$f"; continue; }`. `access request` then refuses a second filing by itself, because `st != none`.

- Treat `j.state === 'pending' || j.state === 'submitted'` as done, with the detail 'requested; waiting for <lab_admin>'.

The grid is also inconsistent with itself. An HF or GitHub host that cannot be reached prints "rejected or unreachable", and `requirements` blocks on it because it greps for `^HF_TOKEN ok` and `^GITHUB_TOKEN ok`. When api.anthropic.com cannot be reached, the student passes.

The laptop and the grid disagree. In extension/src/core/wizard.ts:339, `if (res.status === 401 || res.status === 403) return { ok: false, ... network: false }`. Then line 404 warns "Please create a new one" and does not store the token. Every other non-2xx code is stored as "will be verified on the grid". So a 403 blocks on the laptop, while on the grid it passes as "present".

stepLabAccess (wizard.ts:534) does not check the token again on the laptop. It only runs `ashley access requirements --json`, so the grid's lenient check is the gate that actually applies.

The docs confirm that no real setup-token has been tried (docs/CHECKPOINT_2026-09-28.md lines 27-28, 48 and 252), so nobody knows which code a valid token gets. A 403 is plausible, not just theoretical: a setup-token is a narrower-scope OAuth token, and Anthropic answers scope failures with 403 permission_error. If that happens, every student is stopped at the laptop token step.

Two limits on impact:
- The inbox is 1733 and ingest only checks who owns the file, so a student can write `inbox/$USER.json` by hand and skip `requirements` entirely. The check is a convenience gate, not a security boundary.
- The admin still approves every request by hand.

The proposed fix points the right way but is incomplete. It leaves 5xx passing, and changing wizard.ts:339 for every service would also stop rejecting 403 for GitHub and HF, which is not needed.

confirmed.title: Admin approve/remove from the extension is capped at 120 s while acl_grant walks every file under shared/
confirmed.scenario: acl_grant runs `setfacl -R` plus a `find -exec setfacl -d` over each container sandbox (a full Debian image, tens of thousands of files, one CephFS MDS setxattr each) and over anything else the lab later puts in shared/. Past 120 s, run() kills ssh. The admin sees an empty or truncated message and the list still shows 'pending'. If setfacl prints an error after the disconnect, it dies of SIGPIPE mid-walk and leaves partial ACLs. If the admin clicks Approve again, a second walk runs concurrently. Whether one container actually exceeds 120 s is not measured.
confirmed.fix: Give `access admin approve|deny|remove|reset` no timeout, or a long one. Alternatively, run the ACL walk on the grid under `setsid nohup`, write the status only when it finishes, and have the extension poll the status.

verdict.reason:
This is real, and low severity. The cap is there as described. `gridApi.ts:84` has `access(args)` → `this.ashley(['access', ...args], { timeoutMs: 120_000 })`. In `shell.ts` `run()`, `setTimeout(() => { timedOut = true; child.kill(); }, opts.timeoutMs)` kills the ssh client, and `access()` then returns only `(r.stdout + r.stderr).trim()`, with no check on `timedOut`.

The work is proportional to the number of files. `acl_grant` (`grid/ashley:448-457`) runs `setfacl -R -m "u:$1:r-X" "$c"` and then `find "$c" -type d -exec setfacl -d -m ...` on every entry of `$SHARED` except `access/`. `$LIBRARY_ROOT` = `shared/ashley` holds apptainer `--sandbox` directories built from `docker://node:22-bookworm` (`bootstrap.sbatch:33,35,69`). That is the full buildpack-deps Debian image, on the order of tens of thousands of files, and each one costs a synchronous CephFS MDS setxattr. `npm-<name>`, `cache` and `npm-cache` sit under the same root, and the library can hold more than one container (the GPU variant). Deny, remove and reset call `acl_revoke`, which walks the whole tree too, even for a student who was never granted. Whether one container really passes 120 s is not measured, but it is plausible, and two containers or later lab data make it likely.

The consequences need two corrections to the finding. The ssh is non-pty, so killing the client does not signal the remote command. `setfacl` prints nothing on success and `find`'s stderr goes to `/dev/null`, so in the normal case the walk keeps running on the grid. It then writes `status/<id>.json` and dies of SIGPIPE only at the final `echo`. The "partial ACL via SIGPIPE" case arises only when `setfacl` writes an error, and that path fails with `die` anyway.

What the admin does see is a blank `showInformationMessage('')` (`extension.ts:494-496`). The loop then re-lists, and the student still shows 'pending' while the walk runs in the background. If the admin reacts by clicking Approve again, a second walk runs at the same time; that one is idempotent and harmless. If the admin clicks Deny, Remove or Reset instead, `acl_revoke` races the grant that is still running. The last `write_status` wins, and the ACLs can end up partly granted under a 'denied' status, or the status can read 'approved' after the deny. The 'Grant a user directly' path (`extension.ts:486`) has the same cap.
verdict.corrected_fix: In `GridApi.access`, give the mutating admin actions no cap. Use `const long = args[0] === 'admin' && ['approve','grant','deny','remove','reset'].includes(args[1]); const r = await this.ashley(['access', ...args], { timeoutMs: long ? 0 : 120_000 });`. `timeoutMs: 0` is falsy, so `run()` sets no timer, and the spread overrides `ssh()`'s default. Alternatively use a generous cap such as 30 min. If `r.timedOut`, return an explicit line saying the grid may still be applying ACLs and to wait before acting again. Wrap both call sites (`extension.ts:486` and `:494`) in `vscode.window.withProgress` so the admin sees that it is running. To stop a Deny or Reset from racing a grant that is still running, whether it was left by a timeout or started by a second client, serialize the mutating admin actions on the grid. For example, `exec 9>"$ACCESS_ROOT/requests/.lock"; flock 9` at the top of the approve, deny, remove and reset branches. That directory is mode 700, so only the admin can open the lock. The `setsid nohup` plus polling design is not needed.

confirmed.title: Content moved or copied into shared/ after an approval never reaches approved users, and there is no way to resync
confirmed.scenario: 'Future folders inherit' holds only for entries created in place. If the admin does `mv /rs/rs_grp_oschome/go2432/data shared/` (a rename keeps the source's ACL), or uses `rsync -a` or `cp -p` (which re-chmod files and so tighten the mask), approved users see the name, because they have r-x on shared, but get EACCES inside. Their state still says approved and nothing re-applies the grant.
confirmed.fix: Add `access admin sync`, which re-runs acl_grant for every status file whose state is 'approved', and call it at the end of `library publish`. Document it as the step to run after adding data to shared/.

verdict.reason:
Mostly real, but low severity, and two parts of the finding are overstated or wrong.

What holds up:
- `acl_grant` (grid/ashley:448-456) does two things. It sets a default ACL on `$SHARED`: `setfacl -d -m "u:$1:r-X" "$SHARED"`. Then it walks the entries that exist right now: `for c in "$SHARED"/*; do ... setfacl -R -m "u:$1:r-X" "$c"; find "$c" -type d -exec setfacl -d -m ...`.
- A default ACL only applies to an inode when it is created. `rename(2)` keeps the inode, so it keeps that inode's own ACL. So after `mv /rs/rs_grp_oschome/go2432/data /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared/`, `data` has no `u:<student>` entry.
- `cp -p` fails the same way. So does `mv` falling back to a copy on EXDEV, which can happen across CephFS quota realms. On CentOS 7, coreutils 8.22's `copy_acl` overwrites the inherited access ACL (and, for directories, the default ACL) with the source's plain ACL. That removes the named entry outright.
- An approved student is not in the `oschome` group, so they reach the moved tree only through its "other" bits. If the tree is group-only (2750/2770/640, like the admin's private tree), they can see the name, because `shared/` gives them r-x, but get EACCES inside it.
- Their status file still says `approved`, and nothing re-applies the grant. The code comment ("future folders inherit") and docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:174-175 ("folders the admin adds later are covered too") promise more than this.

What is overstated or wrong:
1. "No way to resync" is not true for a single user. `approve` does not check the current state (lines 558-562): it calls `acl_grant "$id"` again, and that covers everything now in `shared/`. So `ashley access admin approve ID`, or Grant in the queue, fixes one user today. What is missing is a bulk command and any instruction to run one.
2. `rsync -a` does not drop the entry. It chmods to the source mode, which sets the mask from the source's group bits, so a group-readable source stays readable. It only fails when the source itself is group-unreadable.
3. Hooking the resync onto `library publish` is wrong:
   - `cmd_library publish` only runs `sbatch` and returns (lines 76-78), so a sync at its end runs before the job has written anything.
   - The publish path is already covered. bootstrap.sbatch sets `TMPDIR`/`APPTAINER_TMPDIR="$ROOT/tmp"` and builds `$SANDBOX.part` under `$ROOT/containers`, both inside `LIBRARY_ROOT`, which already has default ACLs. Apptainer's rename from the tmp bundle into place stays on the same filesystem, so the inherited entries carry over.
   - It then runs `chmod -R g+rX "$ROOT"` (bootstrap.sbatch:118), which widens the mask. So published containers reach approved users without a resync.

Related but separate: content moved in with o+rx is readable by every grid user, not only approved ones, because `shared/` is 2771.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Add a bulk re-grant to `cmd_access admin`, and do not tie it to `library publish`:

```
sync)
  local f u
  for f in "$ACCESS_ROOT"/status/*.json; do
    [ -s "$f" ] || continue; u=$(basename "$f" .json)
    [ "$(status_state "$u")" = approved ] || continue
    acl_grant "$u" && echo "$u re-granted" || echo "$u: setfacl failed"
  done;;
```

Add `sync` to the `access admin` usage string.

Correct the claims in the line 448 comment and in docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:174-175 and INSTALL.md. Folders created inside `shared/` inherit the grant. Content moved in with `mv`, or copied with `cp -p` or `rsync -A`, keeps its own ACL, so run `ashley access admin sync` afterwards. Until then, `ashley access admin approve ID` re-grants a single user.

An optional extra is an "Apply access to new content" button on the admin queue page that runs `sync`. Do not run `sync` on every `admin list`: it runs a recursive setfacl over whole container trees for every approved user.

confirmed.scenario: After `access init` sets shared/ashley to 2770, the admin follows INSTALL.md 'For leads' and publishes the next container (`ashley library publish --name claude-cuda ...`). Line 76 runs `chmod 2775 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"`, which gives shared/ashley other r-x again. shared/ is 2771, so any grid user can reach it. The current library.json was written by job 40486610 before init with umask 022 (644), so `lib_readable` is true for every account. An unapproved user's `ashley install` adopts the lab container without a request, `access request` answers 'you can already read the shared library', and every sandbox, npm prefix and cache under it can be listed. confirmed.fix: Line 76: `chmod 2770 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"`, or chmod only when `mkdir` just created the directory. Under the single-gate layout described in the shared/ finding below, this line becomes harmless.

verdict.reason: I could not refute this finding: the scenario works against the code as written. In C:/Users/grego/OneDrive/Desktop/ashley/grid/ashley, `cmd_library publish` runs `mkdir -p "$LIBRARY_ROOT" ...` and then, at line 76, `chmod 2775 "$LIBRARY_ROOT" 2>/dev/null`. Once line 76 reopens the directory, any grid user can therefore traverse shared/ (o+x), list shared/ashley (o+rx) and read library.json. `lib_readable() { [ -r "$(lib_file)" ]; }` then returns true for them. `cmd_install` (line ~124) does `if [ $build_own -eq 0 ] && lib_readable && cmd_adopt "$(lib_default)" ...; then return 0; fi`, so an unapproved user adopts the lab container without filing anything. `access request` short-circuits with `lib_readable && { echo "you can already read the shared library"; return 0; }`. Any later publish (a new container, or a republish for a new Claude Code version) therefore reopens the library, and nothing closes it until `access init` is run again. The proposed fix is correct. verdict.corrected_fix:
grid/ashley line 75-76 in cmd_library publish: create the directory without the world bits and set the gated mode every time.

Setting 2770 on a directory that carries ACLs sets the mask to rwx, so named-user r-x grants keep working. The umask covers the case where a group-member lead, not the admin, creates shared/ashley: that lead is the owner and would otherwise leave it at 755. Optional defence in depth, so the gate does not rest on a single mode bit: in grid/bootstrap.sbatch's LIBRARY=1 branch, next to `chmod -R g+rX "$ROOT"`, add `chmod -R o-rwx "$ROOT" 2>/dev/null`.
