confirmed.title: Workers bind only shared/ashley, so the lab folder does not exist inside an approved student's Claude worker
confirmed.scenario: The admin adds /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared/datasets, and approved students get r-X on it through the default ACL on shared/. A student asks their worker to read it and gets 'No such file or directory' inside apptainer. The reason: cmd_adopt (grid/ashley line 93-95) binds `-B $HOME -B $LIBRARY_ROOT` (a student has no /rs/rs_grp_oschome/$USER), and the template adds only $LIBRARY_ROOT. /rs is not bound by default on this grid: commit a38812e shows the publish job hit ENOENT on shared/ until it was bound explicitly. So 'approval opens the lab folder' holds in a Remote-SSH shell but not in the Claude worker, which is how students actually work.
confirmed.fix: In the template, bind the parent when it is readable: `SH=$(dirname "$LIBRARY_ROOT"); [ -r "$SH" ] && BINDS="${BINDS:-} -B $SH"`. This also covers students already adopted with the old BINDS. In cmd_adopt (line 95), bind `$SHARED` instead of `$LIBRARY_ROOT`.

verdict.reason:
The finding holds; I could not refute it. The worker runs Claude, and therefore every tool Claude calls, inside the container: worker.sbatch.tpl:45-47 is `exec "$RUNTIME" exec $NV "${BIND_ARR[@]}" -B "$SCR:/tmp" "$SANDBOX" ... node ashleyd.js`. BIND_ARR comes only from config.env BINDS, plus line 31, which adds `-B $LIBRARY_ROOT` and nothing else, and only when the sandbox sits in the library.

- **Adopted students.** cmd_adopt (grid/ashley:93-95) writes `-B $HOME`. It adds `-B /rs/rs_grp_oschome/$USER` only if that folder exists, which it does not for a student. It then adds `-B $LIBRARY_ROOT` (/rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared/ashley). ROOT defaults to $HOME/ashley (default_root, line 43), so no third bind is added.
- **Students who built their own container.** bootstrap.sbatch:60-62 binds neither the library nor shared/.
- **Is /rs bound by default?** No. Commit a38812e is the evidence: before it, a ROOT under /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared/ashley was not bound, and npm install hit ENOENT on the library path. Nothing in the tree binds /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared itself.

The design and the docs promise more than that. grid/ashley:426 says the lab folder holds "containers now, anything else the lab adds later". docs/ARCHITECTURE.md:168-175 and docs/INSTALL.md:108 say approval opens "the whole lab folder" and "folders the admin adds later are covered too". acl_grant does grant the host permission (a default ACL on shared/ and r-X on its children). But inside the worker, /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared exists only as the bind scaffold around ashley/, so shared/datasets returns ENOENT. It works in a plain Remote-SSH shell and fails in the worker.

The proposed fix is right in substance and is safe:
- Binding shared/ exposes nothing new. The admin's tree /rs/rs_grp_oschome/go2432 stays unbound.
- access/ keeps its 1733/711/700 modes inside the container.
- The `-r` test passes only for group members (2771 gives the group rwx) and for approved users (ACL r-x), so revoked and unapproved students are skipped.
- The template change is the part that matters. It also covers students whose config.env already holds old BINDS and students who built their own container. The cmd_adopt change is optional.

It needs one refinement: guard against adding the same bind twice. If cmd_adopt is changed to write `-B $SHARED`, the template line as proposed would add it again. Use the same case guard that line 31 already uses.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In grid/worker.sbatch.tpl, after line 31 and before BIND_ARR is built (line 44), add:
SH=$(dirname "$LIBRARY_ROOT"); if [ -r "$SH" ]; then case " ${BINDS:-} " in *" -B $SH "*) ;; *) BINDS="${BINDS:-} -B $SH";; esac; fi

This covers adopted, own-build and already-adopted students on their next `ashley worker start`. It never binds all of /rs or /rs/rs_grp_oschome, so the admin's private tree stays out.

Optionally, in grid/ashley cmd_adopt (line 95), write `binds="$binds -B $SHARED"` in place of `-B $LIBRARY_ROOT`. SHARED is assigned at top level (line 437) before dispatch, and the library path is still reachable through that bind. Also note in docs/INSTALL.md that a worker picks up newly granted lab folders only when it restarts.

confirmed.title: Any grid user can take a student's request file name in the world-writable inbox
confirmed.scenario: inbox is 1733, and request names are AccessIDs, which anyone can see through getent or squeue. User X runs `mkdir -m 700 /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared/access/inbox/ab1234.json` (or touches a 644 file with that name). When ab1234 reaches 'Join the lab', line 525 fails with 'cannot write the request' (EISDIR or EACCES). If X uses a 666 file instead, the write succeeds and the wizard says 'requested'. Ingest then sees owner X != ab1234 and archives the file as rejected, so ab1234 stays at 'none' with no explanation. Ingest cannot clear a directory either: line 535's `rm -f` fails on a directory and it is skipped on every run. The student stays blocked until the admin notices and renames it by hand.
confirmed.fix: File under a name nobody can guess, and match the name against the owner: `f=$(mktemp --suffix=.json "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox/$USER.XXXXXX") && chmod 644 "$f" && printf ... > "$f"`. In ingest use `u=$(basename "$f" .json); u=${u%%.*}` and keep the owner == u check. A name someone created in advance can then never collide with a real request.

verdict.reason:
The finding holds; I checked it against grid/ashley.

**How the squat works.** `access init` sets the inbox to 1733 (line 487: `chmod 1733 "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox"`). Any grid user can create any name in it but cannot list it. The student always writes to a fixed, guessable name (line 525: `... > "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox/$USER.json" || die "cannot write the request"`). AccessIDs are public through `getent passwd`. The sticky bit stops the student from removing or renaming a file someone else owns.

**What each squat does:**
- **Directory, or a 644 file owned by X.** The redirect fails with EISDIR or EACCES, and the student sees "cannot write the request".
- **666 file owned by X.** The write succeeds and wizard.ts line 550 reports 'requested'. At ingest the owner check fails (line 537: `if [ "$owner" != "$u" ] ...`) and line 538 moves the file to `requests/rejected.X.*`. No status file is written, so `status_state` stays `none` and `stepLabAccess.check` shows 'not requested yet', with no explanation.

**Which squats clear themselves.** Ingest frees a file squat, because the admin owns the directory and line 538's `mv` succeeds. X can re-create it in a login-node loop, though.

**The directory squat never clears.** The glob on line 532 matches it and line 535 (`if [ -L "$f" ] || [ ! -f "$f" ]; then rm -f "$f"; continue; fi`) runs `rm -f` on a directory. That fails on every ingest. If X leaves a file inside a 700 directory, the admin, who is not root, cannot empty it or `rmdir` it at all. The student is blocked until someone intervenes by hand.

**The proposed fix is right in substance.** Nobody can pre-create a random mktemp name, and the owner check still ties the file to the user. mktemp and `--suffix` exist in CentOS 7's coreutils 8.22.

**What it leaves open.** mktemp creates the file 0600 and empty. An ingest that runs between the mktemp and the printf would accept a 0-byte file owned by the student. The student has no file yet at that point, so the owner check passes and a pending status is written with an empty note and date. After that, line 540 `rm -f`s the student's real request. A small change closes this: write to a hidden temp name that the `*.json` glob does not match, then rename it into place. corrected_fix gives the exact lines.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Student side, replacing line 525. The random name cannot be squatted, and it only appears as *.json once it is complete:
  local t; t=$(mktemp "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox/.$USER.XXXXXXXX") || die "cannot write the request"
  chmod 644 "$t" && printf '{"user":%s,...}\n' ... > "$t" && mv -n "$t" "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox/${t##*/.}.json" || { rm -f "$t"; die "cannot write the request"; }
Ingest, line 534: take the user from the part before the first dot, and keep the owner == u check unchanged:
  u=$(basename "$f" .json); u=${u%%.*}
Optional, line 535: stop retrying `rm -f` on something that is not a regular file:
  if [ -L "$f" ]; then rm -f "$f"; continue; fi; [ -f "$f" ] || continue
A leftover squatted directory is then only clutter; it no longer blocks anyone.

confirmed.title: Approve stops halfway when any file under shared/ belongs to someone other than the admin
confirmed.scenario: ab5188, the other oschome member and a lead, creates shared/ab5188-data (shared/ is 2771 and group-writable) or any file in shared/ashley (2770). The admin approves ab1234. Line 449 grants r-x and a default ACL on shared/. The loop then reaches ab5188-data, which sorts before ashley, and `setfacl -R` gets EPERM because only a file's owner may set its ACL. `|| return 1` triggers `die "setfacl failed"`. ab1234 can now list shared/ but cannot read the library, their status stays pending, and every retry fails the same way.
confirmed.fix: Do not stop on a per-file EPERM: run `setfacl -R -m "u:$1:r-X" "$c" 2>>"$ACCESS_ROOT/requests/acl_errors.log"` without `|| return 1`, and report the paths that failed. Better, use the single gate below, where approve is one setfacl on shared/, which the admin owns.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute it. The scenario works against the code as written in grid/ashley.

- **Other members can write there.** `access init` sets `chmod 2771` on shared/ and `chmod 2770` on shared/ashley. Both are group-writable, so any oschome group member can create entries in them. `library publish` (commented "leads only") does `mkdir -p "$LIBRARY_ROOT"` and then submits bootstrap.sbatch. That script builds `$ROOT/containers/$LIB_NAME` with a plain `build --sandbox` (no fakeroot), so every file in it belongs to the lead who published it.
- **The grant stops on the first failure.** `acl_grant` (lines 448-456) grants shared/ first (line 449), then walks `for c in "$SHARED"/*`, and line 454 runs `setfacl -R -m "u:$1:r-X" "$c" || return 1`. Only a file's owner or root can set its ACL, so setfacl gets EPERM on anything another member owns and exits non-zero. `set -uo pipefail` has no `-e`, but the explicit `|| return 1` still ends the function.
- **The caller dies before writing the status.** Line 561 is `acl_grant "$id" || die "setfacl failed for $id"`, and `die` exits before `write_status "$id" approved` runs.
- **What the student is left with.** They keep `r-x` plus a default ACL on shared/. Because "ab5188-data" sorts before "ashley", the library is never reached and stays unreadable. Their status stays "pending", and every retry fails the same way.
- **It fails even without a sibling folder.** If the other lead published a container inside shared/ashley, `setfacl -R` sets the ACL on the admin's files, fails on the lead's, and returns 1. Approve still dies.
- **New approvals keep failing.** The default ACLs only cover users approved before a file was created. So once another member has created anything, every later approval fails.

**First part of the proposed fix: works, but incomplete.** Dropping `|| return 1` and logging the errors lets approve finish, because `setfacl -R` carries on past per-file errors. But the files another member owns are still unreadable to the student. When that is a container a second lead published, `cmd_adopt` fails `[ -x "$sandbox/usr/local/bin/node" ]` and the student is "approved" but blocked. The fix needs to name those paths and their owners.

**Second part ("one setfacl on shared/"): does not work as stated.** shared/ has to stay `o+x` so students who are not yet approved can reach shared/access/inbox. With `o+x` on shared/, an ACL on shared/ only controls listing it, not entering the folders inside it. Each child would then need its own ACL, which brings the same EPERM back, or be open to everyone. The single gate has to be a separate folder the admin owns, alongside access/.
verdict.corrected_fix:

  find "$c" -user "$USER" -exec setfacl -m "u:$1:r-X" {} + ; find "$c" -user "$USER" -type d -exec setfacl -d -m "u:$1:r-X" {} +

confirmed.title: shared/ is closed only where each child's own mode closes it; folders made before the first approval are readable by everyone
confirmed.scenario: access init closes only shared/ashley (2770). shared/ stays 2771 (others may traverse) and has no default ACL until the first approve. Suppose the admin, with umask 022, runs `mkdir shared/datasets` and copies data in before approving anyone. The folder is 2755 with 644 files, so any grid user who guesses the path (datasets, data, models) can read it. The default ACL that the first approve adds does not change modes that already exist, so the folder stays open. The same happens at any time to a folder moved in with 755 modes. confirmed.fix: Use a single gate, which matches the 'one folder in ceph' intent. Set `chmod 2770 shared`. verdict.reason:

1. Init only closes one child. `access init` runs `chmod 2771 "$(dirname "$LIBRARY_ROOT")"` (line 484), which leaves o+x on shared/. It then runs `chmod 2770 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"` (line 485). Nothing else under shared/ is touched, so every other child keeps whatever mode it was made with. The only default ACL comes from `setfacl -d -m "u:$1:r-X" "$SHARED"` in acl_grant (line 449), which runs on the first approve. Before that, `mkdir shared/datasets` under umask 022 gives 2755 with 644 files. Anyone who guesses the name can then do `cat /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared/datasets/...`, because shared/ is --x for others. A default ACL added later does not rewrite modes that already exist. Trees brought in with `mv`, `cp -a` or `rsync -a` keep or re-apply their 755/644 modes at any time. So "only shared/access is open" (header comment, lines 427-428) depends on how each child happened to be made.

2. The code reopens the one child that init closes. `ashley library publish` runs `chmod 2775 "$LIBRARY_ROOT" 2>/dev/null` (line 76) every time a container is published. After any publish that follows init, shared/ashley is o=r-x. The bootstrap job writes with the default umask; it only adds g+rX (bootstrap.sbatch line 118) and never removes o. So library.json and the sandboxes become readable by every grid user. `lib_readable` (line 53, `[ -r "$(lib_file)" ]`) then returns true for everyone. `access request` prints "you can already read the shared library" and the approval gate is gone. You do not even need the hypothetical mkdir for this.

3. The proposed single-gate fix is right in principle but incomplete as written. With shared 2770 plus `u:ID:r-x` on shared only, an approved student is not in the group, so they fall into the "other" class on shared/ashley. Line 485 still sets shared/ashley to 2770, so the student would get through shared/ and then be refused at shared/ashley. They could never adopt a container. "Contents keep ordinary o+rX modes" only holds if init stops closing the child. The fix also needs to carry the existing drop-box across.

Put a single gate on shared/, and open everything beneath it to "other":
- init (lines 484-487): `chmod 2770 "$SHARED"`. Replace `chmod 2770 "$LIBRARY_ROOT"` with `chmod 2775 "$LIBRARY_ROOT" && chmod -R o+rX "$LIBRARY_ROOT"`. Children must be o+rX, because the ACL on shared/ is now the only thing that admits an approved student. Line 76's `chmod 2775` then becomes correct and can stay.
- Move the drop-box out of the gate: `ACCESS_ROOT="$(dirname "$SHARED")/access"`. The volume root is already o+x from line 482. In init, move any existing area first with `[ -d "$SHARED/access" ] && [ ! -e "$ACCESS_ROOT" ] && mv "$SHARED/access" "$ACCESS_ROOT"`, then apply the same 711/1733/711/700 modes.
- acl_grant: `setfacl -m "u:$1:r-x" "$SHARED"` only. Drop the -R, the per-child loop and the default ACLs.
- acl_revoke: `setfacl -x "u:$1" "$SHARED" 2>/dev/null; setfacl -d -x "u:$1" "$SHARED" 2>/dev/null`. Any stale per-child entries left by earlier -R grants are harmless once shared/ blocks traversal.
- bootstrap.sbatch line 118 (LIBRARY=1): use `chmod -R g+rX,o+rX "$ROOT"`, so a publish under a restrictive umask still reaches approved students.
- Update the layout comment (lines 431-437) to match.

If the per-child design is kept instead, the minimal alternative also has to change line 76 to `chmod 2770`. Otherwise every publish reopens shared/ashley. It would also still leak through any mv, cp -a or rsync -a into shared/.

confirmed.title: Content moved or copied with `cp -a` into shared/ after an approval is unreadable to approved students, and nothing re-applies grants
confirmed.scenario: The admin shares an existing dataset with `mv /rs/rs_grp_oschome/go2432/data/X /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared/`. On the same CephFS this is a rename, and default ACLs apply only when a file is created. X keeps 2750/0640, group oschome, with no u:ab1234 entry. `cp -a` does the same: it copies the source's minimal ACL and removes the inherited entries. ab1234 is approved but not in oschome, so they get EACCES, while `access whoami` still says granted. Only users approved after the move are covered, because `setfacl -R` runs only at approve time.
confirmed.fix: Add `access admin sync`, which re-runs acl_grant for every status/*.json with state approved. Call it at the end of library publish and document it for use after adding content. Under the single gate, the fix is instead one `chmod -R o+rX` on the new content that does not depend on any user.

verdict.reason:
The finding holds, with one condition: the moved content must not already be world-readable, and keeping it that way is what the design wants. acl_grant (grid/ashley:448-456) runs only from `admin approve` (line 561). It sets `setfacl -R -m u:ID:r-X` on the entries that exist under shared/ at that moment and adds default ACLs to the directories (`setfacl -d -m ... "$SHARED"` and `find "$c" -type d -exec setfacl -d -m ...`). Default ACLs apply only when a file is created. A rename keeps the object's existing ACL. The admin tree go2432 and shared/ are on the same CephFS, so a `mv` from one to the other is a rename. On EXDEV (across quota realms) mv falls back to a copy that keeps mode and ACLs, just as `cp -a` does. gnulib's copy_acl turns a trivial source ACL into the destination's access ACL and deletes the inherited default ACL on directories. So group-only content (for example 2750/0640, group oschome) moved into shared/ has no u:ID entry. An approved student outside oschome is then "other" and gets EACCES. Meanwhile `access whoami`/`status` still report granted=true, because that only tests `lib_readable` (library.json). Nothing re-applies the grants automatically. The only workaround is to press "Approve" again for each approved user in commandAccess, which re-runs acl_grant (there is no state check), and nothing tells the admin to do that. The comment on line 448, "future folders inherit", is true only for content created in place. If the moved content is o+r instead, the student can read it, but so can every user on the node who knows the path, because shared/ is 2771 (o+x) for the drop-box. That breaks the closed-folder intent, so either way the default-ACL mechanism does not cover content that is moved in.

Two parts of the proposed fix are wrong. (1) Calling sync "at the end of library publish" is unnecessary and in the wrong place. cmd_library publish (lines 70-78) only submits an async sbatch, so a sync there would run before the build. The build itself happens entirely under shared/ashley: TMPDIR, APPTAINER_TMPDIR and the .part sandbox are all under $ROOT (bootstrap.sbatch:43, 69-70), and a rename inside that tree keeps the inherited entries. The job then ends with `chmod -R g+rX "$ROOT"` (bootstrap.sbatch:118), which restores the ACL mask, so approved users already inherit published containers. (2) The "single gate" `chmod -R o+rX` does not fit this code. shared/ must stay o+x so everyone can reach access/inbox, so o+rX content would be readable by any user on the login node, not only approved ones.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Add an admin subcommand that re-applies the grants for every approved user, and make it keep going past per-file failures. acl_grant stops at the first setfacl EPERM, for example on a file owned by another lead. In cmd_access admin's case:

  sync)
    local f u bad=0
    for f in "$ACCESS_ROOT"/status/*.json; do
      [ -s "$f" ] || continue; u=$(basename "$f" .json)
      [ "$(status_state "$u")" = approved ] || continue
      acl_grant "$u" || { bad=1; echo "sync: some setfacl calls failed for $u (files not owned by $USER?)" >&2; }
      echo "re-granted $u"

Add "sync" to the usage string. Change the acl_grant comment to say that inheritance covers content created in place, and that content moved in (mv, cp -a, rsync -A) needs `ashley access admin sync`. confirmed.title: Approve and remove walk every inode under shared/ inside a 120 s ssh call
confirmed.scenario: acl_grant and acl_revoke run `setfacl -R` plus `find -exec setfacl -d` over all of shared/ except access: the ~1.8 GB node sandbox with its caches, the documented CUDA container, and any datasets. Each call is a synchronous CephFS metadata operation. Once the tree reaches a few hundred thousand inodes, Approve in the extension (`grid.access`, timeoutMs 120_000) kills ssh. The admin sees an empty toast. On the grid the walk either keeps going or dies on SIGPIPE at its first stderr write, so status may or may not become approved. A second click starts a second walk alongside the first.
confirmed.fix: The single gate makes approve one setfacl. Otherwise, run the grant detached on the grid (`setsid nohup ashley access admin approve ID >log 2>&1 &`) and have the extension poll status/<id>.json, or at least raise the timeout for approve, remove and reset.

verdict.reason:
I could not refute this. The mechanics all hold as written. The one thing I cannot measure is the CephFS setxattr rate, so the exact inode count at which a call passes 120 s is an estimate.

1. The cost grows with every inode under shared/. `acl_grant` (grid/ashley:448-456) runs `setfacl -R -m "u:$1:r-X" "$c"` and then `find "$c" -type d -exec setfacl -d -m ...` for each child of shared/ except access/. `acl_revoke` (458-465) does the same walk with `-x`. Deny, remove and reset all call `acl_revoke`, so even denying a pending student who never had an ACL walks the whole tree.

2. The tree is designed to grow. bootstrap.sbatch puts a full Apptainer sandbox (node:22-bookworm is about 1.1 GB, tens of thousands of files), `npm-cache/` and `cache/` under shared/ashley. ARCHITECTURE.md says "an update is a new entry", so each Claude Code or image bump adds another sandbox. The docs also name CUDA and R/Bioconductor entries and "anything the lab adds later". Every setxattr that is not buffered is a synchronous MDS request. At roughly 1 to 3 ms each, a few hundred thousand inodes plus the directory pass takes well over 120 s.

3. The client gives up at 120 s. `access()` in gridApi.ts:83-86 uses `timeoutMs: 120_000`; on timeout shell.ts calls `child.kill()`. `access()` never checks `r.timedOut` and returns the trimmed, empty stdout+stderr. extension.ts:494-496 then calls `showInformationMessage(out.split('\n').pop() ?? out)`, which shows an empty toast.

4. The remote walk keeps going. The ssh has no pty, so killing the client does not stop the command until it writes to a closed pipe. On success setfacl writes nothing and find's stderr goes to /dev/null. In approve, `write_status "$id" approved` (line 562) runs before the `echo`, so status becomes approved when the walk finishes. If setfacl hits an error (for example a file owned by another lead), its stderr write gets SIGPIPE and approve returns 1; the `die` then dies on SIGPIPE too, so status stays pending. So status "may or may not" become approved, as the finding says.

5. Nothing prevents a second walk. The `for (;;)` loop re-lists, the row still shows pending, and nothing locks approve. A second Approve starts a second walk. Worse, if the admin clicks Deny or Remove instead, the revoke walk races the grant walk. The student can end up with ACLs on part of the tree, and the grant's later `write_status approved` can overwrite "denied".

The proposed fix is incomplete. Raising the timeout only moves the threshold. Detaching the walk without a lock keeps the approve/deny race. "Single gate" is right in principle, but it does not work while shared/ is 2771: `other` can traverse shared/ because access/ lives inside it.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Make approve and revoke touch one inode, so no call depends on tree size.

1. Move the drop-box out of shared/: set `ACCESS_ROOT="$(dirname "$SHARED")/access"`. The volume root is already 2771, so everyone can still reach it.

2. In `access init`, make shared/ the only gate and open everything below it to "other" once:
   - `chmod 2770 "$SHARED"`
   - `chmod -R o+rX "$SHARED"/*`
   - `setfacl -d -m o::rX "$SHARED"` (later files inherit it)
   - Also make bootstrap's `chmod -R g+rX` into `a+rX`.

   Content below the gate is reachable only by someone who can traverse shared/, so o+r there does not open it to others.

3. Replace the tree walks with single calls:
   - `acl_grant`: `setfacl -m "u:$1:r-x" "$SHARED"`
   - `acl_revoke`: `setfacl -x "u:$1" "$SHARED"`

   Group members keep access through the group bits. /rs/rs_grp_oschome/go2432 stays 2750.

4. If the recursive walk is kept instead, it needs three things:
   - Run approve, deny, remove and reset under one `flock "$ACCESS_ROOT/requests/.lock"`.
   - Detach the walk (`setsid nohup ... >log 2>&1 &`) and write status "working" first.
   - In the extension, check `r.timedOut` in `access()` and poll `status/<id>.json` rather than showing an empty toast.

confirmed.title: After approval, the tree shows 'Grid installing' with a spinner indefinitely
confirmed.scenario: Take an approved student who has not adopted yet. `status --json` gives ready=false, awaiting_access=false (the library is now readable) and bootstrap_job=''. tree.ts lines 81-83 then show 'Grid installing / installing' with a spinning icon, while the access node says 'granted'. Nothing adopts until the student reruns the wizard or starts a worker, so they wait for a build that will never come.
confirmed.fix: In cmd_status, before computing fields: `if ! is_ready && lib_readable; then cmd_adopt "$(lib_default)" >/dev/null 2>&1; load_cfg; fi`. worker start already does this. Alternatively, report a granted state that the tree renders as 'Lab access granted: start a worker'.

verdict.reason:
The finding holds, but the proposed fix needs one correction.

**Why the scenario works.** A student on the access path ran `cmd_install` while the library was unreadable. That path only runs `set_cfg AWAITING_ACCESS 1` and returns (grid/ashley:127-130). No bootstrap job is submitted, so BOOTSTRAP_JOB stays empty and no READY file is written. After the admin approves, `acl_grant` makes `shared/ashley/library.json` readable. `cmd_status` then reports:
- `ready=false`, because `is_ready` needs READY, CLAUDE_BIN and the sandbox node (line 31).
- `awaiting_access=false`, because line 208 requires `! lib_readable`: `if [ "$ready" = false ] && ! lib_readable && [ -z "$BOOTSTRAP_JOB" ] && [ -d "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox" ]; then awaiting=true; fi`
- `bootstrap_job=""`.

tree.ts lines 81-83 therefore show 'Grid installing', description 'installing', icon 'sync~spin'. The access row shows 'granted', since `who.granted` is `lib_readable`. Nothing on the status or tree path adopts. Only three things do:
- `worker start` (line 253);
- the wizard's `stepLabAccess.check` when `j.granted` (it runs `ashley install`);
- re-running `stepGridInstall`, whose check now returns 'todo', 'scripts present, container not built'.

So the spinner lasts until the student happens to click one of those. It is a real but low-severity display problem, not a hard block, because clicking the access row or 'start one' does adopt.

**Problem with the proposed fix.** `cmd_adopt` fails through `die()`, which is `exit 1`. Called directly inside `cmd_status` in the same shell, any adopt failure would abort `ashley status --json` with no output. The stderr is redirected away too. Adopt can fail even when `lib_readable` is true, for example when:
- library.json has no "default" entry;
- the sandbox's `usr/local/bin/node` is not executable through the ACL mask;
- `claude_bin` is unreadable.

`GridApi.status()` then returns `{error: ''}` because `r.code !== 0`, and tree.ts:76-77 shows 'Ashley not installed on the grid' with an Install button. That is worse than the spinner. The adopt has to run in a subshell. `worker start` line 253 has the same silent-exit pattern, but that is outside this finding.
verdict.corrected_fix:
In cmd_status (grid/ashley:198-202), adopt in a subshell before the fields are computed, so that a `die` inside cmd_adopt cannot kill the status command:

  load_cfg
  if ! is_ready && lib_readable; then ( cmd_adopt "$(lib_default)" ) >/dev/null 2>&1; load_cfg; fi
  local ready=false cv="" bst=""
  is_ready && ready=true

If status should stay read-only, fix only the display instead. Status already emits "library":true, so in tree.ts:81-83 add a branch before the 'Grid installing' fallback. When !st.ready && !awaiting_access && !st.bootstrap_job && (st as any).library, show 'Lab access granted' with the description 'start a worker to use the lab container', icon 'pass', and the command ashley.workerStart. worker start already auto-adopts.

confirmed.title: No test shows that named-user ACLs are enforced for a non-owner, on the login node or on compute nodes
confirmed.scenario: The only test approved go2432 on directories that go2432 owns. The kernel checks an owner against the user:: entry and never consults u:go2432, so the test shows that setfacl stores the entry, not that CephFS grants a non-owner access through it. Compute nodes may also mount CephFS with different options. If a node's mount ignores ACLs, `lib_readable` is true on the login node, but the student's worker exits with 'REFUSING: sandbox ... incomplete'.
confirmed.fix: Test with ab5188 before relying on it: `mkdir t; chmod 700 t; setfacl -m u:ab5188:r-x t`. Named-user entries are checked before group entries, so ab5188's oschome membership does not hide the result. Have ab5188 run `ls t` on the login node and `srun -p reqp --qos=requeue ls t` on a compute node.

verdict.reason:
The gap is real, and it is low severity. Access depends entirely on named-user ACLs. acl_grant (grid/ashley:449-458) does `setfacl -m "u:$1:r-x" "$SHARED"` and `setfacl -R -m "u:$1:r-X" "$c"`, and shared/ashley is 2770. A student outside oschome therefore reaches the container only through the u:ID entry.

The only recorded test of that entry is docs/CHECKPOINT_2026-09-28.md:59: "Tested as go2432: approve added `user:go2432:r-x` + default ACL". Line 65 adds: "Not simulated: a real second user filing a request (needs another grid account)". Under the POSIX ACL check, an owner is matched against user:: and the named entry is never consulted. So the test showed that setfacl stores the entry, not that CephFS enforces it for anyone else.

The failure path in the finding matches the code. `lib_readable() { [ -r "$(lib_file)" ]; }` (line 53) and `[ -x "$w_sandbox/usr/local/bin/node" ]` (line 269) are both evaluated on the login node. The job then runs `[ -x "$SANDBOX/usr/local/bin/node" ] || { echo "REFUSING: sandbox $SANDBOX incomplete"; exit 1; }` (worker.sbatch.tpl:33) on a compute node. If that node's CephFS client does not enforce ACLs (for example ceph-fuse without client_acl_type=posix_acl), the student falls back to the "other" bits of a 2770 directory and the worker refuses. Whether any node is actually mounted that way is not known from the repository; the point is that nothing has checked.

The proposed test is wrong for the case it is meant to catch. CHECKPOINT line 106 says `getent group oschome` = ab5188, go2432, so ab5188 is in oschome. A directory made anywhere under the setgid 2771 volume inherits group oschome. After `chmod 700 t; setfacl -m u:ab5188:r-x t`, the ACL mask becomes r-x and the mode's group bits show r-x (drwxr-x---+). If a mount ignores ACLs, ab5188 still gets in through those group bits, so the test passes in exactly the case it should fail. "Named-user entries are checked before group entries" is only true when ACLs are being enforced.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Run a negative control, which works even though ab5188 is in oschome. As go2432, in /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared: `mkdir acltest; chmod 750 acltest; setfacl -m u:ab5188:--- acltest; getfacl acltest`.

Then, as ab5188, run `ls /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared/acltest` on the login node and `srun -p reqp --qos=requeue ls /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared/acltest` on a compute node. The named entry is enforced only if both are refused with "Permission denied". If either succeeds, access came through the group bits and that node ignores ACLs.

Optionally, add a positive check that ab5188 does not get from its group. `chgrp` a second directory to a group ab5188 is not in (check with `id ab5188`), then `chmod 700` it and `setfacl -m u:ab5188:r-x` it. ab5188 should be able to list it on both nodes.

Also run the worker's own check on a compute node: `srun ... test -x <sandbox>/usr/local/bin/node && echo ok`. Remove the test directories afterwards. Write the result in the checkpoint, replacing the owner-only test at line 59.

confirmed.title: The world-writable inbox uses the lab's CephFS quota, and ingest keeps the junk
confirmed.scenario: CephFS quotas apply to a directory tree, not to a user, so any grid user can write gigabytes into inbox (for example `dd if=/dev/zero of=inbox/x.json bs=1M count=100000`) or use it as private storage. The files cannot be listed and stay until the next ingest. Ingest then moves oversize or foreign files into requests/ instead of deleting them, so the space stays charged to the lab volume until the admin finds and deletes the files by hand.
confirmed.fix: In ingest, `rm -f` anything rejected instead of `mv` (keep only the owner-matched request of 4 KB or less), and append one line (owner, size, name, time) to requests/rejected.log so there is still a record.

verdict.reason:
The finding holds, and it is worse than described. `access init` makes the drop-box writable by every grid user: `chmod o+x "$vol"`, `chmod 2771` on shared, `chmod 711 "$ACCESS_ROOT"; chmod 1733 "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox"`. Any user can therefore create files of any size under /rs/rs_grp_oschome, and CephFS charges quota to the directory tree, not to the user who wrote the file.

Ingest runs only when the admin opens the queue (gridApi.ts:74, `access admin list --json`), so junk sits there until then. When ingest does run, rejected files are kept, not deleted. Line 538 reads `mv -f "$f" "$ACCESS_ROOT/requests/rejected.${owner:-unknown}.$(date +%s).json" 2>/dev/null || rm -f "$f"; continue`. That branch catches both a foreign-owned file and one larger than 4096 bytes (line 537, `[ "$(stat -c %s "$f")" -gt 4096 ]`). A same-filesystem mv is a rename, so every byte stays charged to the lab volume and the file keeps the attacker as owner. The scenario `dd if=/dev/zero of=inbox/x.json bs=1M count=100000` works exactly as stated.

The proposed fix is incomplete, for three reasons:
1. The loop only visits `for f in "$ACCESS_ROOT"/inbox/*.json` (line 532). A file named `blob`, `x.bin`, `x.json.part` or `.hidden` is never matched, so ingest never touches it. It stays attacker-owned, readable and writable by the attacker, and cannot be listed by anyone but the admin. That is free private storage on the lab quota that the "rm -f the rejects" change never reaches.
2. A directory named `x.json/` fails `[ ! -f "$f" ]`, and the `rm -f "$f"` that follows cannot remove a directory. If the attacker creates it mode 700 and fills it, the admin cannot empty or delete it at all. The admin owns inbox but has no write permission inside the attacker's directory, so only root can clear it.
3. Nothing in ingest limits how much can be written between admin visits. Any grid user can fill the lab's 20 TB allocation, and every lab job then fails with EDQUOT. Deleting at ingest time only cleans up afterwards.
verdict.corrected_fix:
Change the ingest loop so it checks every entry in the inbox, not only `*.json`, and deletes whatever it does not accept, logging each deletion:
```
while IFS= read -r -d '' f; do
  b=$(basename "$f"); u=${b%.json}; owner=$(stat -c %U "$f" 2>/dev/null); sz=$(stat -c %s "$f" 2>/dev/null)
  if [ "$b" = "$u.json" ] && [ -f "$f" ] && [ ! -L "$f" ] && [ "$owner" = "$u" ] && getent passwd "$u" >/dev/null && [ "${sz:-99999}" -le 4096 ]; then
    : # existing accept path (status check, mv to requests/$u.<ts>.json, write_status pending)
  else
    printf '%s owner=%s size=%s name=%q\n' "$(date -u +%FT%TZ)" "${owner:-?}" "${sz:-?}" "$b" >> "$ACCESS_ROOT/requests/rejected.log"
    rm -rf -- "$f" 2>/dev/null || echo "cannot remove inbox/$b (owned by ${owner:-?}); needs root" >&2
  fi
done < <(find "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox" -mindepth 1 -maxdepth 1 -print0)
```
Also show the admin how full the inbox is, for example `du -s "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox"` in `admin list` output.

Say plainly that ingest cannot stop the quota from being filled between admin visits, and cannot clear a mode-700 directory an attacker plants. Only two things bound that:
- A directory quota on the inbox, `setfattr -n ceph.quota.max_bytes -v 1048576 "$ACCESS_ROOT/inbox"`, if the site's CephFS client capabilities let the owner set one. Otherwise ask the grid admins to set it.
- Moving the world-writable drop-box off the lab's quota tree altogether.

confirmed.title: On the grid, status/ is still 755, so anyone can list who requested access
confirmed.scenario: CHECKPOINT_2026-09-28 records `status 755` from the 03:53 init run; the code now says 711. Until init is rerun, any grid user can list shared/access/status and read every student's request note and the admin's deny or remove messages.
confirmed.fix: Rerun `ashley access init`. It is idempotent: it only chmods, and `mkdir -p` does nothing for directories that already exist. This makes status/ 711.

verdict.reason:
I could not check the grid itself, so this rests on the checkpoint and git history. The drift is real. docs/CHECKPOINT_2026-09-28.md line 52-54 records that `ashley access init` ran at 03:53 UTC and set `shared/access/{inbox 1733, status 755, requests 700}`. The 711 change came later, in commit e348145 at 00:07:38 -0400 (04:07 UTC). The code now reads `chmod 711 "$ACCESS_ROOT/status"` (grid/ashley:487). Nothing in the checkpoint (updated 04:20) or anywhere else in the repo records init being run again. So until someone reruns it, status/ is still 755 and any grid user can list it. That shows which AccessIDs asked for lab access, and each file can then be read.

Rerunning init is safe. It is idempotent: `mkdir -p` does nothing to existing directories, and every chmod only adds or narrows bits. The rerun has to use the current script, though. The commits are local (last push 3969234), so first check that ~/.ashley/bin/ashley on the grid is the e348145+ version.

The fix is incomplete, because 711 only stops listing. It does not stop reading. `write_status` runs `umask 022` (line 444), so every status/<id>.json is 0644 and world-readable, and the file names are grid AccessIDs. Those IDs are easy to learn: they have a fixed format, and `who` or `ps` on the shared login node shows the logged-in ones. Students in the same lab also know each other's. So even with status/ at 711, any user can run `cat /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared/access/status/<id>.json` and read that student's request note and the admin's deny or remove message. That goes beyond the design intent ("each student reads status/<own id>.json").
verdict.corrected_fix:
1. Make sure the grid runs the current grid/ashley (e348145 or later). Then rerun `ashley access init`, or run just `chmod 711 /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared/access/status`.
2. Make each status file readable only by the admin (the owner) and the student it names. In write_status, replace `umask 022` with `umask 077` and grant the student read access on the .part file before the mv:
   write_status() { umask 077; printf ... > "$(status_file "$1").part" && setfacl -m "u:$1:r" "$(status_file "$1").part" && mv "$(status_file "$1").part" "$(status_file "$1")"; }
   (The student reads their own file through status_state/whoami/status, which the ACL allows. The admin owns the file and still reads all of them in `admin list`.)
3. Fix any files already there, once: `for f in /rs/rs_grp_oschome/shared/access/status/*.json; do [ -e "$f" ] || continue; chmod 600 "$f"; setfacl -m "u:$(basename "$f" .json):r" "$f"; done`

rejected.title: The rule 'request only after every step works and tokens verify' is checked only on the student's side
rejected.reason:
Refuted: the bypass is real, but it is not a security problem. Nothing in the admin's view says a request was checked, so the scenario does not hold.

1. **The bypass works.** The ingest loop in grid/ashley (about lines 532-545) only checks that the file is a regular file, `owner == u`, `getent passwd "$u"` succeeds, it is 4096 bytes or less, and `status_state "$u" = none`. It never looks at `requirements`, so a hand-written `inbox/ab1234.json` owned by ab1234 is accepted.

2. **The gate cannot be enforced on the server, and it is not meant to be.** `cmd_access requirements` runs `cmd_verify_tokens` as the student, against tokens kept in the student's own private home. `grid/ashley` is the student's own copy under `~/.ashley/bin`, so the student can edit it. The admin's ingest cannot read another user's tokens, and should not. Any "verified" signal would be something the student reports about themselves, and the student can fake it. The design already accepts this: the one-request rule and identity are checked at ingest, and readiness is left to the student.

3. **Skipping the gate gains the student nothing.** Approval is still the admin's decision about a named, owner-checked user. The ACLs `acl_grant` hands out are the same whether or not the student's tokens work. A student who skips the gate only gets an environment that does not work for them yet. No other user, token or file is exposed.

4. **The admin is not told requests are verified.** In extension.ts `commandAccess`, each queue row shows only the state, `note:`, `requested` and `message:`. There is no verified label, so a skipped-gate request is not shown "exactly like a verified request". The queue also offers "Grant a user directly — no request needed", so the admin workflow does not assume a request means anything was checked. The docs (manual.md:125, 00_getting_started.md:38, INSTALL.md:105) describe the gate to the student, as a readiness step. They make no promise to the admin.

5. **The proposed fix would add nothing.** Ingest cannot tell a request filed through `ashley access request` from one written by hand, because both are owned by the student and look the same. It would therefore write `"verified":false` on every request, a field that carries no information.

At most, the doc comment at wizard.ts:494 ("so only working environments join") overstates things. That is wording, not a vulnerability.

rejected.title: The 'every step done' requirement is checked only in the student's own process, and the admin cannot tell
rejected.reason:
The bypass does work mechanically, but nothing it enables is a defect, and the proposed fix adds no assurance.

1. The bypass works. `request` checks requirements only in the student's own process, at grid/ashley:522: `cmd_access requirements >/dev/null || { ...; die "finish the setup first..." }`. At ingest (lines 532-544) the only checks are that the file is a regular file, not a symlink, owned by the user it names, 4096 bytes or smaller, and that the user has no status yet (`[ "$(status_state "$u")" = none ]`). Then it runs `write_status "$u" pending "$n" "" "$c"`. So `printf '{}' > shared/access/inbox/$USER.json` becomes a pending request. It is not shown "exactly like" a verified one, because it has no note and no requested time, but a forger can add both.

2. The bypass harms nobody. The owner check (`[ "$owner" != "$u" ]`) means a student can only file for themselves. Nothing is granted until the admin runs `admin approve`, which calls acl_grant, so the admin's decision is the real gate. The requirements check is only there so that working environments join (wizard.ts stepLabAccess: "so only working environments join"). A student who skips it gets, once approved, read access they would have been given anyway. The only cost is a broken setup on their own side. No other user and none of the admin's private files are affected.

3. The grid-shell case is not a gap in the grid code. `ashley access request` typed in a grid shell still runs the grid-side checks at line 522: token verification and the bashrc block. What it skips is `extraRequirements` (store.ts:105-114: the VS Code extension list, Remote-SSH and the MCP bridge). Those are facts about the laptop, and the grid cannot observe them.

4. The proposed fix does not work. Embedding `requirements --json` in the request is still self-reported. The same one-line forgery can write `"requirements":{"ok":true,"missing":[]}`, so the admin still cannot tell a checked request from an unchecked one. `requirements --json` also covers only the grid side, so the laptop items this finding names would still be missing from it. What the fix would actually label is requests from older clients, which is not the scenario described.

This is an inherent limit of a check that runs on the student's side, which the design already accepts ("The admin cannot re-verify the student's tokens"). It is not a concrete problem in the code.
